subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When
the debate was adjourned last night, Mr. Speaker, I was indicating the reasons why I felt justified in holding that there could not be any priority in the matter of direct taxation either for the central government or the governments of the various provinces. I then quoted sections 91 and 92 of the constitution, and I also showed the part played by subsidies in the first years of confederation.
Leaving now that aspect of the matter, I would like to revert to the social consequences of the solution to the existing problem between the government of Quebec and the government in Ottawa with respect to the fiscal agreements which were signed, or could have been concluded with regard to fiscal matters, to say that it would entail enormous difficulties from a constitutional point of view. However, if the parties concerned must live up to the constitution, it is equally important to appraise the social and economic responsibilities which constrain the Canadian government to retain for itself its main source of revenue, that is, direct taxation.
Reading through the history of confederation, from 1868 to the present day, we will not fail to realize quickly what increase there has been in the responsibilities of the federal government, both as far as the people of this country themselves are concerned and as regards international relations which have

gained tremendously in importance since those days.
In 1868 the population of this country was approximately 3,700,000 whereas it now is over 15 million. In 1868 the total revenue of the federal government was $13-6 million, whereas in 1952, it rose to close to four billion dollars.
At the time of confederation we were a colony. Now we have become an adult nation which must live up to responsibilities which no government desiring to retain and respect its own national autonomy can escape.
Since 1868, the provinces which pioneered confederation have been joined by six other provinces. Together they now make up this Canadian nation of ours. Of course we have not come this long way together without stresses and strains, and great difficulties to overcome.
When paying tribute to the fathers of confederation, it is appropriate also to appreciate the wisdom of those political figures who, since 1868, have led our country within the framework of the confederative system so that today we may pride ourselves on being Canadians.
But I am digressing and I come back to the argument I wish to make, that is, that the social obligations of the Canadian government in a partly planned economy are closely connected with the use of the direct tax and the use of that field of taxation is definitely not the exclusive possession of a political party or an innovation of the present government.
In 1917 the Canadian government exercised for the first time its constitutional right to tax the income of its citizens in view of the expenditures due to our contribution to world war I. Incidentally, a Conservative minister of finance, who was a member of a union cabinet, proposed that measure himself on behalf of the government then in power.
From 1920 to 1934, the revenue from that new source of taxation hardly changed from year to year. In 1920, those direct taxes brought to the Canadian government $64-5 million, as compared with $61-3 million in 1934.
As will also be remembered a depression then so violently shook the country that several provinces were forced to approach the central government in order to cope with the unemployment crisis that broke over the whole country.
Then came the period of social security legislation, when the Canadian government had to take over responsibilities in the form of financial burdens that time could only increase.
The Budget-Mr. Maltais
First, it was the old age pension legislation in 1927, which the province of Quebec, then under Liberal rule, refused to accept, invoking the principle of autonomy, but that was agreed upon nine years later by a Union Nationale government, as a political advantage out of which sufficient capital has been made since. Then we had legislation concerning unemployment insurance, pensions for the blind, family allowances, in a word a whole set of social measures that is absorbing about a third of the Canadian government's budget.
It is the duty of the national government to maintain a sound national economy and, while respecting the constitutional rights of the provinces, the Canadian government cannot, without running the risk of encountering serious troubles, give away its revenue sources without a previous agreement. It is now possible through our social legislation to eliminate partially the special inequalities which tend to spring up and grow under a democratic system based on private enterprise where economic conditions vary in a more or less pronounced degree between the different areas of our country.
Nobody will deny the sense of responsibility the government has shown when it introduced this legislation providing as it were for the distribution of more than a billion dollars to the Canadian population. When we think that the province of Quebec received, last year, apart from the war veterans allowances, nearly $200 million by way of social benefits, we can realize the tremendous effort put up by this government to avoid a possible unemployment crisis.
In 1953, Quebec children received 107 millions; our 70-year-old citizens, 69-9 millions; those aged 65 to 70, 39-8 millions; and our blind people 1-1 million.
These obligations assumed by the Ottawa government, approved and asked for by all Canadians, are directly connected with the power of taxation on incomes which makes it possible to carry out this social work.
If I take into account the cost of governing this country, the money needed to finance our national debt and the tremendous amount needed for national defence in the face of the communist threat, I am inclined to believe that these national obligations must be considered in the solution of the problem existing between Quebec and the federal government.
In view of the part played by direct taxation in modem public finance, the Canadian government has been forced to rely more and more on this method of taxation, to which it may rightfully resort under our constitution.
4376	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Maltais
Direct taxation has been, for several years, in the hands of the central government not only an efficient means of collecting revenues but also a control lever for the administration, stabilization and guidance of our national economy.
So it is no wonder that the Canadian government has been under the obligation to depend much more upon direct taxation in the past twenty-five years than during the years which immediately followed the adoption of the confederation act.
Obviously, on account of the equal and concurrent right of the central and provincial governments to that same field of taxation, a reallocation of taxation powers between the various governments has long been wished for.
Since, unfortunately, no such formula satisfactory to all concerned has been found, we have come, for want of anything better, to a temporary compromise, that is to the system of fiscal agreements which was put into effect during the last war and which remained in force with some modifications.
These fiscal agreements aim at two things:
1.	A better apportionment of national revenue between the most favoured province and the less favoured, economically speaking, with a view to enabling the latter to discharge their constitutional obligations in conformity with a principle of autonomy which any province might proudly make its own, and also of making possible a decentralization of the revenues derived from taxation.
2.	The avoidance of double taxation.
In Canada nobody has yet denied that some provinces cannot levy all the revenues they need to fulfil their obligations, even though they resorted fully to the taxation fields granted them by the constitution.
Let those who may be tempted to discount the ill effects of double taxation cast a glance towards the province of Quebec.
This double taxation is today at the root of the trouble we are witnessing in the province where I was born, where I live and where I learned the language I now speak and which, by the way, I have no fear of losing. The government of the province of Quebec, which was represented by its premier at the various federal-provincial conferences at Ottawa, had the opportunity of making counter-proposals to the fiscal agreements but never made any constructive proposals regarding that fiscal policy. In fact, after showing a sincere


desire to co-operate, even to the point of stating its willingness to sign an agreement, the government refused any such agreement. It would seem that it prefers to temporize rather than to act.
Before speaking of the unilateral decision of a majority of the Quebec provincial legislature to levy a direct tax affecting more than 300,000 Canadian taxpayers and before dealing with the request submitted to the Canadian government by a non-political organization, asking that the said tax be deductible, as a Quebec taxpayer I would like to say a few words about the negative stand taken by the Quebec government since 1948.
I am not denying the right of the government of my province to levy a direct tax within the province, even though this is questionable. Moreover, in the absence of any agreement, I would certainly have been in favour of the method suggested by the Montreal chamber of commerce, which asked the Quebec government to levy an income tax of 5 per cent, which would have been completely deductible and would not have cost one cent more to the Quebec taxpayers.
Evidently, the Quebec legislature had a right to levy the tax it wanted, but we were once told that autonomy was not a question of 5 per cent and that principles had no monetary value. Today, we have a 15 per cent tax, of which 5 per cent will be deductible from the federal tax; thus, the cost to Quebec taxpayers will be 10 per cent more.
These figures of 5, 10 and 15 per cent remind me, not of a 5 per cent autonomy, but, as they indicate, of a "5 and 10" autonomy.
The Quebec government refused to sign the agreements. It had a right to do so. But what is the net result? It is as follows:
In 1948, the Quebec government levied, through corporation tax and succession duties, the amount of $43,100,000; in 1949, $59,200,000; in 1950, $61,200,000; in 1951, $71,700,000; in 1952, $84,800,000; in 1953, $80,900,000; in 1954, $82,600,000. This last figure of $82,600,000 is taken from the public accounts of the province of Quebec; in other words, the government of Quebec levied during seven years, though no agreement was signed, the amount of $483,500,000. Let us see now what the Quebec government would have received, if it had signed a fiscal agreement. I include in the following amounts the rental of succession

duties, since the amount produced by this tax was included in the amounts levied by the province of Quebec through its own legislation.
By virtue of these agreements, the government of Quebec would have received in 1948, $45,100,000; in 1949, $64,100,000; in 1950, $69,900,000; in 1951, $78,200,000; in 1952, $107,700,000; in 1953, $111,700,000; in 1954, $121,300,000, that is, all in all, $598 million, or a difference of $114,500,000 which the province of Quebec could have received, but which it has lost.
And that is not all. Since the other nine provinces have already signed agreements with the Canadian government for the next three years, let us see what Quebec will lose by not signing these agreements and taking into account the 15 per cent tax now in operation, let us examine what will happen if the present difficulty persists and if this problem is not solved.
Quebec will receive approximately $23 million this year from its personal income tax, but 5 per cent only of this impost will be deductible from the federal levy. It means that Quebec will receive, during the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1955, without any additional cost to its taxpayers, about $7,800,000, deductible from the federal tax, and it will cost Quebec taxpayers $15,200,000 representing the non-deductible portion; for the fiscal year 1956, Quebec will receive about $7,900,000, deductible and it will cost taxpayers $15,900,000, non-deductible. For the fiscal year of 1957, Quebec will receive about $8 million, being the deductible portion, and it will cost taxpayers $16 million nondeductible.
In brief, the government of Quebec will collect, as being deductible from personal income tax, an amount of $23,700,000 and it will cost taxpayers a further amount of $47,100,000 that the government of Quebec will collect just the same, but which will add to the burden.
If you add to that figure of $23,700,000 the amount Quebec will derive from corporation taxes and succession duties during the same period, you get a sum of $275,700,000, representing the total revenues the province of Quebec will receive from deductible direct taxation.
How much would Quebec get under the temporary agreement system over the same period? Supposing the economic position remains about the same for the next three years, we arrive at an amount of $372 million.
The Budget-Mr. Maltais
Making the necessary deductions, Quebec will therefore, during the next three years, lose the difference between the eventual revenue under the agreements, that is $372 million, less its own deductible taxes amounting to $275-7 million, or a net loss of $96-3 million. Of course, this figure will be partly compensated by the additional burden of $47-1 million, but I am not taking this into account, as this sum will be levied in the province of Quebec, and is not deductible.
As I said a moment ago, the province of Quebec has lost, during a period of 8 years, $114-5 million because it remained outside the agreements, and if the status quo is maintained, the province will lose an amount of $96-3 million during the next three years. Mr. Speaker, since the province of Quebec is going to lose $210 million through maintaining the present situation in respect to fiscal policy up to the time the agreements expire, I am right in saying with my colleagues from Quebec that the problem is serious and alarming.
That sum of $210 million just about equals the budgetary expenses of the province of Quebec for 1951. In other words, the Quebec government would have thus been able to devote to the education and the public health of my fellow Quebeckers twice the amount assigned to those fields in 1951 and would have been in a position to solve without difficulty the problems which confront the universities in Quebec, to say nothing of highways and colonization.
The seriousness of the situation calls for a solution and since the 15 per cent deduction asked for cannot be granted without undermining the very base qf the entire fiscal agreement system now in force between nine of the provinces and the federal government, I shall look elsewhere for a compromise solution which would have the advantage of endangering in no way the existing agreements.
Since the province of Ontario when it signed an agreement did not rent its right to succession duties, would it not be possible to get Quebec, Ontario and the federal government to sign an agreement which would enable those two provinces to collect from that source larger revenues than they are receiving at present?
Such a result might follow a concession on the part of the federal government through which it would reduce the succession duty it is collecting or accept, after negotiation, relatively high rates of deduction with regard to provincial succession duties.
Owing to the fact that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are more favoured than the other eight provinces, the granting of

The Budget-Mr. Maltais that concession by the central government would not materially affect the agreements with the other eight provinces, because they are already drawing subsidies under the tax rental agreements.
In 1947, the largest revenues derived from the taxation rights were received by Ontario and amounted to $15,200,000; Quebec received $11,400,000, British Columbia, $3,200,000 and New Brunswick, $1 million.
Since revenues derived from that taxation field vary greatly as between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario on the one hand and the rest of the provinces, on the other, such a concession by the central government would not entice the other provinces to avail themselves of that concession.
If such an agreement enabled the province of Quebec to amend her succession duties in order to get $7 or $8 million more than she is now drawing from that source of taxation, and avoid double taxation, the present stalemate could be solved by means of another concession on the part of the Quebec government.
As a matter of fact, the government of the province of Quebec is seeking a further revenue of $23 million, the amount which the 15 per cent income tax levied upon its taxpayers is supposed to yield.
As it could already derive approximately $8 million more from its succession duties, the government of Quebec has only to amend its personal income tax so as to lower the rate to the level of 5 per cent deductible from the federal income tax in order to get another $15 million which would not cost one cent more to its taxpayers, as such a tax would be entirely deductible.
Quebec then, without renting its taxation fields, would get the $23 million which it seeks, and double taxation would be avoided.
On the other hand, there would not be any loss of revenue for the federal government, as that portion of the subsidy that Quebec would get by signing an agreement would remain in the consolidated fund of Canada in order to compensate for the loss incurred by the change made in its succession duties.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether such a proposal will be considered, but I believe that no stone should remain unturned if we really want to find a way out of this difficult situation, and I urge the provincial government of Quebec to seek with an open mind and in a spirit of co-operation a common ground for the solution of this fiscal problem.


I am voicing this appeal in all sincerity. I have noticed that at a press conference, on April 9 last, as reported by the Canadian press the next day, the premier of Quebec stated that he would not initiate new negotiations with Ottawa.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said in this house yesterday that the Quebec government had given no answer following the last federal-provincial conference convened by the federal government. Such being the case, I fail to understand why the premier of Quebec does not wish to enter into new negotiations.
There is no need for new negotiations. It should be sufficient to continue those which were started at the last conference, in regard to which the Quebec government has thus far given no answer. To make things clearer I would like to quote the Prime Minister's statement as reported on page 4338 of Hansard:
The statement agreed to after the in-camera discussions, and published at that time,- . . .
That is after the dominion-provincial conference on fiscal agreements.
*-was that each province would consider these tax rental proposals and would indicate its position at a later date. There followed a great many more negotiations between the Department of Finance and the individual provinces, and within eighteen months or so nine of the ten provinces indicated their respective positions and entered into the proposed temporary rental agreements which are to extend to March 31, 1957. The government of Quebec did not do so, however. It just abstained from having any further dealings or discussion with us about the matter in any way or form whatsoever. I saw in the Montreal Star some time ago a report that Mr. Duplessis said that he had written to me and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). He may have written to me and to the Minister of Finance, but not about any solution of the fiscal problems between the federal authorities and Quebec, unless he is referring to some correspondence we had when we were discussing the grants to universities. In one of those letters he said this: Why do you not turn over to me 5 per cent of the personal income tax? That will be more than you are offering to Quebec universities under this $7 million grant. I replied that this grant would expire on March 31. I do not remember just the date of the correspondence but it was some little time before March 31. I said: You know that under the present act we cannot make any remission of this 5 per cent of income tax to the provincial government. We could merely give it as a deduction to a taxpayer who had paid a provincial income tax to your government. The other thing is the constitutional lapsing of this vote unless Quebec's share is taken from it before March 31. Can we not find some scheme which will not prejudice your position or ours but which will not leave these Quebec institutions without their proportion of this grant which is about to lapse? For that year an arrangement was worked out whereby there was a

joint commission of the federal government and the provincial government to make the allocation and to recommend a way in which the grant would be paid to the institutions in Quebec. But that had nothing to do with the general possible collision between the exercise of federal rights and the exercise of provincial rights in the field of direct taxes.
Mr. Speaker, if words have any meaning at all, and if the dominion-provincial conference of 1950 had the respect of the nine other provinces of my country, I have the right to say that Ottawa never closed the door on negotiations and that if the one-sided action of the government of my province had closed the door, the words of the Prime Minister of my country opened it yesterday.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget is conspicuous on two main grounds. The first is its failure to deal in any way with the changing situation with which Canadians are now confronted. The second is the attitude it displays not only toward the province of Quebec but towards every province of Canada. So far as this budget is concerned there apparently is no unemployment, no serious situation in the textile industry, no great problem in the electrical equipment industry, nor anything to worry those making farm machinery. In fact, the government apparently thinks there is nothing to worry about which will not be cured by the efforts of our friends in Washington. From listening to the obedient desk thumping of the supporters of the government and the bland assurances of the government itself, one would think that there were no problems of any kind to be examined. Yet it is from the official records of the government that we learn of the seriousness of the situation with which we are confronted. As we have been told more than once, 570,000 people are registered as applying for jobs. That does not include everyone who is seeking a job. There is a more important figure when we seek to understand what the buying power of our people is. According to the March figures of the dominion bureau of statistics, which are the last available, the total of unemployed and partially employed was 777,000. That is a formidable figure. That means that according to the government's own figures more than three-quarters of a million of our workers have been greatly reduced in their buying power, with consequent reduction of demand for what other
The Budget-Mr. Drew workers can produce. In fact we have a higher percentage of unemployed or partially employed in Canada than in the United States, in spite of the tremendous development of resources and industrial expansion which is taking place.
We have the greatest wheat carryover in our history. We have the prospects of a better than normal crop this year. Not a word in the budget indicates any recognition of the serious position in which the farmers now find themselves with huge quantities of grain stored on their farms on which they are not able to obtain down payments. Nothing in the budget or the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) indicates any recognition of what this means to the railways, to the shipping companies and, above all, to the farmers themselves, whose difficulties are aggravated by the fact that the government gives them no lead. Not a word is there in the budget to show any real recognition of the tragic plight of the Canadian merchant marine. There is nothing to suggest that this vital part of our international service is to receive any encouragement from this government.
Our manufacturers who are wondering how they are going to increase employment, our fishermen, our producers of base metals, and the farmers who still provide the firm foundation of our whole economy, are blandly assured that there is nothing really to worry about and that anybody who is in any difficulties had better meet the situation by more efficient methods. This, Mr. Sneaker, does come with particularly bad grace from a government which has refused over and over again to take the steps which are necessary to give it some sort of efficien"y in its own operations. It has been said before and will bear repeating that this government refused to adopt the very methods that any business would adopt if it hoped to remain solvent. Yet this government tells businesses that are finding difficulty in maintaining employment today that the way to solve their problem is to be more efficient, and certainly not to follow the government.
There is not a single member of this house who does not know where millions are being wasted by the government. There is not a member of this house who does not know of duplication of services or, to be more accurate, of multiplication of services. Merely as a symptom, and not in any way as a measure of the disease, it is only necessary to examine the number of economists, statisticians and publicity agents that this government needs to proclaim its virtues.
4380	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew
Over and over again we have introduced a motion asking for the setting up of a body of inquiry similar to the Hoover commission in the United States. As a result of that commission in the United States, according to the statements that have been made, $7 billion has already been saved and they expect to save another $5 billion. On a proportionate basis that would mean a saving of nearly $700 million here and the hope of still more.
I recognize that it is not possible to say in exact figures what savings a similar inquiry could assure here. However, I do suggest that it is not sensible for anyone to suggest that considerable savings cannot be made having regard to the manner in which our government has operated in so many ways along lines similar to those followed in the United States. We have heard figures placed before us of substantial savings that could be made. After all, those relate to some subject that is before us with the figures attached to that item by the government. What I am emphasizing is that there is a broader basis of saving, the kind of saving that every big business undertakes periodically if it has any hope of maintaining its sound economic position. Whatever the figure would be it would certainly run into hundreds of millions of dollars. Without any serious examination of the proposition and with nothing but an arrogant denial that anything can be improved, the government has simply asked its supporters to vote down this motion time and time again.
Yet this is the government which now tells the people of Canada that their answer to the problem they face is to be more efficient in their production and in their daily work. When the government prescribes this cure, well might we remind them of the adage, "Physician, heal thyself". This inefficiency of government, and the firm refusal of the government to deal with it in any practical way, is related to the second important aspect of the budget. As the government has continued to centralize power, the checks and balances provided by the federal system have been more and more weakened and the opportunity to restrain extravagance and waste has become less and less. It is for that, as well as for constitutional reasons, that we should examine the attitude of the government toward the provinces and the municipalities. I say that in the firm belief that the closer we bring the supervision of public expenditure to the people themselves at the provincial and municipal levels, the more effective the supervision of the spending is going to be.
In many ways this subject is the most important part of the budget speech. The Minister of Finance regarded it as sufficiently


important to devote a very considerable part of his speech to an explanation of the negative attitude adopted by the government. The refusal to consider the proposal for tax deductions in respect of the personal income taxes levied in the province of Quebec is important not only in its effect upon the income taxpayers of the province of Quebec but upon the people of every province because of the attitude it discloses towards the earlier undertakings of this government. Four weeks ago today I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to invite the premiers of the provinces to attend a conference to discuss our acute tax problems. At no time did I suggest, as was indicated yesterday, that the Prime Minister of Canada invite the premiers to come together to assist him to solve the particular problem with the province of Quebec. That, after all, would have been an affront to the government of Quebec, and it certainly would have placed upon the premiers of other provinces a responsibility that is not theirs.
I urged the Prime Minister to call a conference because the situation arising in relation to the province of Quebec is merely a symptom of the general problem. Yesterday the Prime Minister gave his answer. It was a most unhappy speech in every way. It was unhappy in content, unhappy in presentation and unhappy in its consequences.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A very good speech.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In effect it was a simple and emphatic statement that until the province of Quebec submits to terms imposed by this government there will be no conference, although every province has been asking for a conference for a long time.
There were some curious omissions from the statement of the Prime Minister. He quoted with satisfaction and at considerable length the statement of the premier of Ontario at Quebec in September, 1950-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At Ottawa.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At Ottawa in 1950-some considerable time before Ontario had signed an agreement, but he failed to make any reference to the statement of the premier of Ontario at the time the agreement was signed. While that may not have been the intention of the Prime Minister, the effect of his quotation yesterday and his speech generally was to leave the impression that Ontario is satisfied with the present situation. For that reason let me quote from what the premier of Ontario said at the time the agreement was signed. This was the text that accompanied the announcement of that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think it was 1952.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, 1952.
The signing of this agreement will not solve Ontario's tax problems. It is, at best, a stop-gap, pending the working out of a more satisfactory distribution of tax and revenue sources. Nor does the agreement provide a solution to the municipal problem which is, in turn, dependent on a shift of taxes and revenues from the federal government to the provinces and from the provinces to the municipalities.
We have urged the federal government to begin discussions with the provinces now with a view to obtaining these objectives. The present tax system is outmoded. The rapid growth of industry and population in Ontario has created enormous demands for provincial and municipal public services in the form of new hospitals, schools, highways, sewers, water-works and projects for conservation and pollution control. But in the face of this expansion, the tax structure has remained immobile and out of balance with the requirements of the provinces and municipalities.
Our object should be to achieve a tax structure that is favourable to industrial expansion and gives full play to the willingness and power of the people to work and save. At the same time it should be clear, equitable and in balance with the need of each level of government. We must aim not only at social justice in taxation, but also at devising a system which best assures that economy and efficiency in government services will be encouraged.
At the dominion-provincial conference of 1945-46, an economic committee, consisting of technical advisers of the federal and provincial governments, was established and accepted as permanent machinery by all the governments to serve as a fact-finding body on taxes and other fiscal matters. This economic committee held meetings in December, 1945, and again in January, 1946, but its work was not continued.
We urge the federal government to re-constitute this economic committee. The committee should then be directed to study the Canadian tax structure, including the distribution of taxes and revenues and the allocation of functions among governments, and to report on the fiscal measures which will best serve to promote good government at all levels.
I would point out that at the very time the government of Ontario entered into this tax agreement, it pointed out the agreement was nothing but a stopgap. The premier of Ontario made it quite clear that this was not something he expected to stand until some time nearer the approach of the time to reconsider this agreement. He said, and I repeat words that I have already quoted:
We have urged the federal government to begin discussions with the provinces now with a view to obtaining these objectives.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this statement is not open to the interpretation that the government of Ontario, any more than any other provincial government, expects to wait until the maturity of the present agreement or until all provinces have similar agreements to examine the situation. It will be seen that the premier of Ontario asked that the economic committee reconvene when he made 83276-277
The Budget-Mr. Drew this statement in 1952. The purpose of this economic committee was to provide the essential statistical information upon which to base arrangements between the governments. As evidence that the position of the Ontario government has changed in no way on this subject, the request for the convening of the economic committee was repeated by the premier of Ontario in his budget speech in March of this year. This was brought to the attention of the federal government. I have no doubt, in fact, that they had already seen it. On March 22, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was asked if the government had made any decision concerning the proposals by the premier of Ontario that the economic committee be reconvened. The minister's reply, as reported at page 3195 of Hansard for that date, was certainly illuminating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As usual.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He said:
Speaking for myself, I have not been able as yet to give any consideration to that suggestion.
As the Minister of Finance says, it was as illuminating as usual.
Having received no satisfaction from the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), who had asked the first question, then asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on March 26 if the government had made any decision in regard to this proposal. The Prime Minister replied, and these are his words, as reported at page 3364 of Hansard for that date:
Mr. Speaker, the matter has not been discussed in council and, of course, no decision has been arrived at.
There the matter stands. Nearly two months have passed since the proposal was made, but there is still no answer. Evidently the decision has not yet been made or has been made against the proposal. The Prime Minister would lead us to believe that the decision has been not to call a conference because he says he sees no reason for bringing the representatives of the provinces together. In his speech yesterday the tone of the Prime Minister was conciliatory in every way, and so were his words. According to the Prime Minister the door is open. The question arises, open to what?
Can there be any doubt in the mind of anyone who has listened to the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that the door is open only if the government of Quebec is prepared to accept some arrangement similar to the temporary agreements with the other provinces? The speech of the Prime Minister yesterday, taken as a whole, is not susceptible to any

The Budget-Mr. Drew other interpretation. The Prime Minister asked the government of Quebec to make a proposal. Now, whether the proposal is agreeable to the government of Canada or not, the government of Quebec has made a proposal. We have all read about it for some time, and we have heard it discussed in this house. It was discussed by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech.
The government of Quebec proposes that the 15 per cent personal income tax levied by that government be deductible for federal tax purposes so that there will be no duplication of taxes. Whether this proposal is acceptable to the Prime Minister or whether it is approved by other hon. members in this house, there is no doubt of the fact that there is a definite and understandable proposal which has been refused. It is that situation with which we are now confronted. I submit it is our duty to examine this. We must examine it. The Minister of Finance took a great deal of time to explain why they were refusing this proposal. It is the duty, therefore, of every one of us to consider just what this proposal means; what the effect would have been if it had been accepted, to see if we can find any reason for the attitude of the government under present circumstances.
I have sought to emphasize my own belief that this is part of a common problem affecting every province and arising out of the wartime tax agreements of 1942. It is not something peculiar to Canada alone. The same problem does affect the governments of Australia and does affect other federal states as well. At the time the provinces of Canada gave up their rights in the fields of direct taxation allotted to them by the British North America Act, the government of Canada solemnly undertook to restore the position of the provinces in these tax fields after the termination of hostilities. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that this undertaking was not something put forward by the government of Canada on its own initiative. It was something that was insisted upon by the provinces that at that time recognized the possibility that at the time the agreements ended there might not be a return of those tax rights.
As the Prime Minister recalled, I was present here in Ottawa during some of those discussions. As a matter of fact, I renewed those discussions when I became premier of Ontario in 1943. I know what the reasons were, and I know that it was on the prompting of the provincial governments that certain undertakings were given that were intended to be respected after hostilities had ceased. Having said that, may I say without any reservation -that the provinces which entered into those agreements did so in the


belief that they were playing their part in a common effort to give to Canada the opportunity to meet the great dangers with which we were then confronted in the very gravest days of the last war. After the war was over requests were made that these agreements be carried out. In fact, before the final stages of the war with Japan we were called together in conference here in Ottawa to consider proposals put forward by the Canadian government. In fact, it was on the very day that the first atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima that we met here in Ottawa to discuss ways and means by which those undertakings could be carried out. That is now nearly nine years ago. The provinces are still waiting for the government to take the initiative, which must be the initiative of the government of Canada, to find a solution to this financial and constitutional problem, which was the result of the combined effort when all the governments met during the years of war to meet the dangers that then confronted the whole of Canada.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that examining the discussions that took place, examining the agreements that were signed in 1942, examining the statute which approved those agreements and examining all the discussions that have taken place since that time, it is the duty of the government of Canada to find the way to honour that pledge.
Again, let me repeat that this is not an issue between the government of Canada and the government of Quebec alone. This is an issue affecting the whole federal system. It was very simply and fairly stated by the late Angus L. Macdonald in a speech to the Dalhousie law school two years ago in these words:
A fundamental question now arises. It is this: Do we wish to continue as a federal state?
I quote his words because the premier of Nova Scotia at that time was a great student of constitutional law. He had also been closely associated with this problem from its very beginning. That same question is being posed today in Australia. The Prime Minister of Australia said last year that the federal system there will-and I quote his words- "break down hopelessly", unless the authority of the state is restored. I merely quote this to indicate that there are others who have this problem, and that there are others who share the same opinion.
The Prime Minister of Canada said yesterday: What good would come of inviting the premiers of all the provinces to a conference? First, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that it would be fulfilling the duty of the government of Canada to the provinces. Second, is the fact that it would be starting to work out arrangements by which its pledge could be

fulfilled. Third would be the fact that all provinces could discuss this subject with knowledge of the difficulties which will arise if a clear and workable plan is not formulated before the termination of the present temporary agreements.
May I quote one of the most highly respected financial papers in the world in regard to this situation? The London Economist, discussing the agreements signed in Australia in 1942, which followed very much the same pattern as those in Canada, had this to say last year:
No other single act in the history of Australian federalism has done more to strengthen and consolidate the centralization of power in Canberra than the adoption of uniform taxation in 1942.
It was in relation to this statement of the Economist that the late Angus L. Macdonald said this:
If that comment be accurate for Australia, can a like view be taken of the existing federal-provincial agreements in Canada? That is a question to which I should hope all Canadians, and particularly lawyers, should give serious and enlightened consideration.
It is with these warnings and statements of this kind before us that I do urge the Prime Minister and every hon. member to examine this problem with the utmost care and to recognize that what has happened in the case of the province of Quebec is merely an indication of what can happen on a much larger scale, unless the Prime Minister comes to grips with this subject without further delay by inviting all the premiers to a conference.
There is another aspect to this question of a general conference which I should mention in passing. As was recited in the statute approving the agreements of 1942, it was the municipalities as well as the provincial governments which gave up taxing rights. At all times the municipalities have been as greatly concerned with some proper reallocation and definition of taxing power as have the provincial governments. All over Canada today municipal councils are emphasizing the serious situation with which they are confronted. Denied other taxing fields, the increasing local burdens place heavier and heavier taxes upon the homes and real estate generally. If there were no other reason for a general conference at this time this in itself would constitute an urgent and compelling reason why the Prime Minister of Canada should invite the provincial premiers, along with representatives of the municipal councils, to examine this subject without further delay.
If only to emphasize my point, may I recall the statement made by the minister responsible that civil defence organization is more 83276-277i
The Budget-Mr. Drew important than ever before because of the threat of the hydrogen bomb. That was what he said only a little over a week ago. If that is so, and in this case I do not think his statement will be seriously challenged by anyone, then there are added urgent reasons why the plight of the municipalities be examined and a new method found for raising the revenue required by the municipalities as well as in the larger legislative areas.
Now, let me examine the request of the province of Quebec, the proposal of the province of Quebec, that the provincial income tax amounting to 15 per cent of the federal income tax should be deducted. Great exception has been taken to the levy of the 15 per cent provincial income tax. At what point, Mr. Speaker, did 15 per cent become such an impossible figure? The Prime Minister admits that the burdens on the provincial and municipal authorities have increased proportionately with those of the government of Canada. It seems strange that the government of Canada should be so worried about 15 per cent, when it not only approved of an earlier levy of 15 per cent by the province of Quebec, but actually collected that amount for them under a single tax form, with a single cheque payable to the federal treasury and signed by the taxpayer. That system worked well for several years up to the time of the tax agreements in 1942. This government then accepted that percentage as satisfactory and collected the provincial as well as the federal tax under a system which not only worked satisfactorily between the government of Quebec and the government of Canada, but worked equally satisfactorily between the government of Ontario and the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But there was no deduction, of course.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with that. It worked equally satisfactorily with taxes collected from Manitoba and taxes collected from Prince Edward Island. At that time well over 70 per cent of the taxpayers of Canada were paying their taxes under that satisfactory arrangement. And the fact is that, in the case of Ontario, there was no duplication of taxation. At that time the dominion government had not, of course, all the taxes gathered together the way they have today. They were only collecting 39 per cent of the total tax burden. The provincial and municipal governments had a wide field of taxation open to them. Therefore the Ontario government deducted the taxes payable to the federal government from all the taxpayers in Ontario, and avoided duplication. And at the time the
4384	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew 1942 agreements were signed all the governments were discussing the possibility of extending similar arrangements to avoid duplication.
This is not the first time it has been tried. And when it worked so well in the years up to 1942, I would recall the promises to restore the provinces to their position at the time the agreements were signed. And their position at the time the agreements were signed was a position which included this method of collection-a method of collection which has been asked for by the premier of Ontario as well as the premiers of other provinces.
I submit that this government is in honour bound to adopt that method, if it lives up to its undertaking made in 1942 to restore the provinces to their position at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was only 4 per cent in
Quebec in 1942.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At what point did this method become so unacceptable? The fact is that it became unacceptable at the time this government started on a definite plan of the centralization of taxation in Canada to get as much power here in Ottawa as possible. This has been no accident. It has been a steady and deliberate plan to bring under the control of this government as much of the total tax moneys of Canada as possible.
Then we come to the question as to whether the 15 per cent should be deducted. Well, it is not for me, and I submit it is not for the government of Canada, to say whether a provincial government is levying the correct amount, as long as the amount it is levying is within its rights, and for the purpose of carrying out its duties under our constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So long as it complies with those requisitions it has a right to do so. And I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) saying "hear, hear." I would hope that we might see some evidence of complying with that principle. Any talk of a province occupying the whole field is really not worthy of consideration.
The fact is that the provinces are very susceptible to the attitude of the people toward them. The people are much closer to their provincial governments than they are to this government at Ottawa. The provincial governments have not the publicity agents, either, to obscure the realities by the methods that have been employed so successfully by the government. The fact is that the provincial governments will undoubtedly find that voters in any province, if they can, will deal with the situation to meet what is legitimately required for their own purposes.


Now, let us examine the question of deductibility. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicates that he does not question the right of the government of Quebec to levy its income tax. But he does challenge in the strongest terms the proposition that there is any prior claim to the field of direct taxation. I cannot recall that it has been asserted at any time that there is a legal priority on the part of either government. We all know that through somewhat loosely-worded provisions of the British North America Act the federal government was given particular power to tax in any field. The provincial governments were given the right to tax only in the field of direct taxation. That produces one simple result: If the provinces are to have any real authority, then that authority must be interpreted in their ability to tax. Therefore the provinces, having the direct tax only as a source of revenue for the carrying out of their responsibilities, surely must be assured of an adequate area of taxation within that field.
As premier of Ontario, this is what I had to say on the subject on August 6, 1945- and I repeat that statement now as a statement which indicates the position we took at that time, and it was the same position that was put forward by other provinces. I said:
While it might be legally possible for the dominion government to extend direct taxation to such a point that they could completely blanket the only field of taxation open to the provincial governments, it need not be argued that such a result was never intended and that the very existence of the provincial legislatures and their governments under the British North America Act carries with it the implicit understanding that the dominion government will leave the field of direct taxation open to the provinces to such an extent as will make it possible for them to fulfil their obligations to the people.
Mr. Speaker, that puts forward a position that was not seriously challenged at that time. The fact is that the government of Canada has recognized a priority, and it has itself established the principle of deductibility. Why argue about deductibility as though it was something that had not already been accepted by this government? The question is only as to amount, only as to percentage. This government has already provided for 5 per cent in the case of personal income tax, and it has dealt with the subject also in relation to corporation income tax. Deductibility as such, therefore, is not in question; it is the amount.
If we recognize the fundamental principles of our federal system, it is the right of the government of Canada to say to any province: We accept the proposition that you can levy a provincial personal income tax. We re-

cognize that it should be deductible. But we think it is our duty to tell you that it must not be over five per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the acceptance of that proposition would mean the end of the federal system. The acceptance of that proposition would mean that no provincial government could carry on its duty, except with the consent and permission of the federal government. No matter what the name might be, the provincial governments would be nothing more than subservient commissions carrying out the orders of this government. They would be rubber stamps for Ottawa. And whenever they needed more money they would have to come, cap in hand, as the premier of Quebec has been invited to do, through that door that is opened for such a clearly defined purpose.
Surely that was not the spirit or the intent of our federal system. Then, again, let us recall that this government itself gives the strongest arguments in support of the proposal which has been made by the province of Quebec.
This government for some time permitted five per cent deduction in the case of corporation income tax. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec have levied a seven per cent tax. They were two per cent above the provincial taxes, and the five per cent was deductible as in the case of personal income tax.
Last year the government introduced an amendment extending the exemption from five to seven per cent, and for what reason? They extended it because that was the figure of the provincial levy. This was what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said on March 10, 1953, as reported at page 2783 of Hansard:
This amendment is being recommended in conjunction with the proposal which I announced in my budget speech of increasing the credit for corporation income tax from five per cent to seven per cent in accordance with the principle that nothing in federal legislation shall in any way discriminate against a province which does not enter Into a tax rental agreement.
That was a principle clearly asserted in relation to corporation tax which at that time had been set at a figure above the figure for which the federal government had provided deduction. Therefore, for the reasons explained by the Minister of Finance, the deduction was increased to meet the amount imposed by the provincial government. There is no other way by which it could have been arrived at, and the fact is that the only question is one of amount. The only reason that this government will not meet the request for a deduction up to 15 per cent is that five per cent is, so they
The Budget-Mr. Drew say, what the province can have in the case of corporation tax. But it is apparently not for the province to say what they should levy in the field of their own taxation.
If it was proper for the government to extend the deductibility to the point at which the provincial governments had levied corporation income tax, then why is it not equally proper to extend the amount of deductibility in the case of personal income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, because I know he wants to be accurate; but the seven per cent was raised from five per cent after the negotiation of the 1952 agreement. That is the figure provided in the agreement which the provinces may impose.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes; that was the figure provided in the agreement which the provinces may impose for the very simple reason that this government was meeting the levy that was imposed by the government of Ontario and it was made at the suggestion of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the suggestion of the provinces, certainly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was suggested by the premier because the provinces were levying seven per cent and that province as well as the province of Quebec arrived at the figure of seven per cent for the reasons which the Minister of Finance has now indicated. The Minister of Finance has now made it quite clear that there was no other arithmetic foundation for arriving at that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At that time it was a matter of negotiation between all the provinces and that was the figure arrived at.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was a matter of negotiation and I hope there will still be some consideration given to this subject, because I am going to suggest that the same method of negotiation be used in relation to personal income tax as was adopted in the negotiations which took place in regard to corporation income tax.
The government has established the principle of deductibility. It accepted 15 per cent as a perfectly proper percentage on an earlier occasion. Let us therefore examine what the results would be if we followed the same methods of negotiation as were followed in 1952.	*
If this arrangement were carried out, the government of Quebec would receive some $25 million less from this source than it would receive if it entered into an agreement similar to that which the other provinces have signed. The situation therefore is a simple one. The situation is that the proposal
4386	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew put forward by the government of Quebec is one which will cost the Canadian taxpayers generally $25 million less than would be paid if Quebec entered into an agreement at this time, similar to that which this government is so anxious to have them sign.
Since the government of Quebec is prepared to accept $25 million less, and the federal treasury saves that amount, what explanation can there be for the suggestion that any province would be prejudiced by an arrangement of this nature? Yesterday the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 4339 of Hansard:
No one, I hope, would suggest, In order to give Quebec taxpayers more generous deductions tnan those now provided for in our income tax law, that we should either increase the tax rental payments to the other provinces or agree that they too may impose their own taxes and get for their taxpayers, at the very substantially increased expense of the federal treasury, somewhat more generous deductions. The federal treasury just could not stand either of those courses.
I cannot believe, Mr. Speaker, that those were the words the Prime Minister intended to use. It is difficult to understand why they were used. The federal treasury would be paying out $25 million less than they have indicated they are anxious to pay to the province of Quebec. There would not be one cent more paid to any other province. There would be a net saving to the taxpayers of Canada of $25 million which, to be perfectly clear about it, would be at the expense of the income tax payers in the province of Quebec. We cannot complain about that, however, because that is what the government of Quebec has suggested. The situation is that not one cent would be added to the amount that this government -would collect from the other provinces. Is the Prime Minister suggesting that this government really is not ready to have Quebec sign an agreement? I do not believe it. On the contrary, I was under the impression they were anxious to have Quebec sign an agreement. If that is so, then they are prepared to pay Quebec $25 million more without adding a cent to the taxes which would be collectable elsewhere, or change the amount payable by the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What would be the effect of the 15 per cent deduction in Ontario?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the points I am making are, I am sure, perfectly clear to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you answer the question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question that is being asked is as unreal as the statement by the Prime Minister which I have just quoted. Every provincial government has fixed its taxes for
[Mr. Drew.l

this year and the hon. member who has just interrupted should know that. If he does not know that, he should, because they were fixed some considerable time ago, and at the time they were fixing it the premier of Ontario asked the government of Canada to reconvene the economic committee and we are still waiting for this government to decide what it is going to do in regard to that proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have still failed to answer the question.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not failed to answer the question. I have made it perfectly clear that there would be no change this year in the amount that would be collected in Ontario or any other province, not a cent. There cannot be, for the taxes have already been levied and anyone who is aware of taxing methods must know that and would not raise that question.
But, Mr. Speaker, I think there is a solution to this apparent impasse. It is one which would detrimentally affect no provincial agreements. It is one which would detrimentally affect no taxpayer in any part of Canada. I suggest and most earnestly urge that the Prime Minister agree to this deduction. The Minister of Finance indicated this afternoon a method by which this can be dealt with. He indicated that when this government very properly extended the deduction in the case of corporation income tax by the amount levied by the provinces it was done in a friendly co-operative spirit. Now then, let the same method be adopted in regard to personal income tax. Let it be done for this year. Let the Prime Minister at the same time call the premiers together to a conference here and start discussing the vitally important problem-not of the single tax payments in any province but the broad problem-of the reallocation of taxes in every province of Canada for the benefit of the provinces and of the municipalities. That would be a solution that would deal with the situation this year. If this government is ready to send its representatives all over the world to meet other governments in the hope of finding solutions of problems, surely it should be prepared to display the same spirit here in Canada. Surely it does not think that a solution of this difficulty-and I am talking about a solution with all the provinces-is more difficult than is the solution of those problems which arise with the persons that Canadian representatives are now meeting at Geneva.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has it within his power to display a spirit which would be extremely helpful in ending comments of a kind that are not conducive to the

strengthening of unity within this country. The Prime Minister alone can call this conference together. I assume that we shall soon be voting on the budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those "hear, hears" show a greater measure of interest in the budget than most of the hon. members opposite have displayed at any time since it was first announced.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the "hear, hears" from your own side?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have been bored to tears for the last hour.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the solution to this problem is one which need not place before us the necessity for deciding the advantages of one procedure or another. The facts are there. Whether it is the best proposal or not, the proposal before this government is one which will save the taxpayers of Canada $25 million they would otherwise pay if the government of Quebec signed the agreement which this government has sought to have them sign. When the vote on this budget takes place, it is perfectly true that it is not a vote on an ordinary budget. The Prime Minister made that fact clear yesterday. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the fact that the house is anxious to dispose of the budget debate but, as a new member who has not taken up any of the time of the house during this, my first session of parliament, I feel that I should make a few remarks at this time because I represent a constituency which is both rural and industrial. The budget is a document that has considerable influence on the year ahead for both farmers and industrial workers. Before speaking briefly on the budget, there are a few matters I should like to discuss which are of particular interest to the people of my consituency. I want to make these observations because in my riding, where we have some unemployment, I think that certain measures that are of interest both to the provincial and the federal governments will be of some help in relieving unemployment. For example, at the present time the federal and the provincial governments are making a forest survey in connection with the pulp industry. Half the cost of the survey is being met by the federal government. The result of the survey may mean more development in the pulp and paper industry which of course would help to relieve unemployment.
The second point that I should like to bring to the attention of the house is the fact that work will be undertaken in Cape Breton this summer on the trans-Canada highway. I understand that as part of this work a bridge will be built across the Bras d'Or lake which will relieve the congestion caused by the present long wait for ferries.
I might also mention that we have one of the finest national parks in the Dominion of Canada at Ingonish. It is a part of the famous Cabot trail and is a great attraction for


tourists, who come from all parts of North America and spend their vacations at beautiful Keltic lodge.
We also have one of the finest harbours on the Atlantic seaboard. The federal government built a new terminal at North Sydney at considerable cost. There are a large number of men employed as stevedores and in similar work at North Sydney which is the point of embarkation for Port aux Basques, Newfoundland. Within a short time we expect a new ferry, now under construction, to be put into operation between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. This ferry is badly needed because imports and exports over this route have increased considerably since Newfoundland joined confederation. I am pleased to say that the people of my constituency appreciate very much the federal government's action in making the ferry route to Newfoundland part of the Canadian National Railways system.
The port of North Sydney also enjoys a large trade with the Portuguese fishing fleet, and the purchases they make in the town of North Sydney are very important from the standpoint of revenue. We look forward to an increasing and expanding trade with the Portuguese fishermen, but I would remind the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) that some dredging is necessary at several docks to permit continued and uninterrupted service for these foreign fishing boats. I am reasonably sure that the minister will see that this necessary work is undertaken.
The budget is a very important statement. It is an account of the stewardship of the government for the past year and a forecast of the social and economic picture for the year that lies ahead. The budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on April 6 did not make any great changes. There is a great deal of argument that many things might have been done, but in my opinion economic conditions in Canada and throughout the world would seem to justify the stand taken by the government, namely, to determine if the economic factors outside our own country which influence trade and mean so much to us in the field of employment will bring about the changes necessary to stimulate our whole economy.
In order to solve unemployment not only government action is required but also the understanding co-operation of labour, management and government. In the circumstances which now confront the country it would appear to me that the only way to increase our purchasing power and to stimulate consumer buying, which would assist in

relieving the unemployment problem, would be for the government to give immediate reconsideration to the extending of unemployment insurance benefits and to the increasing of social security payments. This line of action, I think, is realistic and completely the reverse of recommendations made by some sections of the opposition that the government should retrench by curtailing its expenditures in many fields.
We have heard a great deal about the proposal of the government of Quebec to impose a provincial income tax of 15 per cent and to have it allowed as a tax offset by the federal government. As a junior member of the house, I am not going to say too much on the question of dominion-provincial relations or the constitution of Canada, but I should like to say that the only way we can get equality of opportunity in Canada, as between province and province, is for the federal government to have the power to collect taxes as they are doing under the dominion-provincial agreements so that we will be able to carry on our present social security program, hospital grants, vocational training grants and other assistance to the provinces of that nature.
In effect, under the dominion-provincial agreements, with the taxing powers in the hands of the federal government, the federal government is then in a position to redistribute the wealth of the country on a more equitable basis. The prairie provinces and the maritime provinces would lose very heavily were any action taken which would tend to upset the present dominion-provincial agreements. I feel that it is my responsibility as a Nova Scotia member to put myself on record as stating most emphatically that I will use whatever power I have as a member to support a continuing policy of a more equal distribution of the wealth of the country.
The budget did offer some relief to the Nova Scotia coal mining industry. The 10 per cent sales tax on stokers for use with furnaces in the heating of buildings, and on coal crushers for use directly in the manufacture and production of goods, was discontinued. This, I think, is a gesture in the right direction.	.
The coal industry of the maritime provinces is undergoing a serious period of reconstruction in order to meet the competition from gas and oil. The picture is far from bright, but I feel the industry, the workers and the general public of Nova Scotia are aware of the problem and are doing all they can locally to find a solution. I feel that the people of the maritimes. with their inherent good sense, their vision and courage, will find
The Budget-Mr. Brooks a way out of this problem as they have out of many other serious problems with which they were confronted.
One could continue, Mr. Speaker, presenting the academic picture of the budget. However, I believe I have said sufficient to indicate that little change will be felt by the average person in Canada in 1954 in so far as tax relief is concerned. I repeat, therefore, what I said in opening, that the government was realistic in holding the line for this year in order to determine what changes may be necessary to meet conditions in a changing world. The next year will be a crucial one. If we can get by without a war, and I am sure we can, then the main emphasis will be on making the social and economic changes that are going to be necessary to meet conditions that are arising as other parts of the world get into production and with whom we shall have to compete in world markets.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I found it necessary to occupy this short time at this period of this session. I did feel that I should make these few observations to indicate to the people who sent me here that I am endeavouring to present their views on matters that are creating difficulties in the country.

They all had great difficulty, as did the hon. member, in finding anything to praise.
A few days ago I listened to the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy). He pointed out that a great many men in his constituency were without work, and said there were a great many out of employment in the city of Moncton as a result of lay-offs by the Canadian National Railways. I have spoken on the Chignecto canal upon many occasions, and like the hon. member for Westmorland, I intend to continue pressing for the development of that canal.
There are, however, immediate problems in the maritimes and, as I said a moment
