The Budget-Mr. Brooks ago, there is little indication that this budget will help us in any way. I listened to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). I might say that I wish to congratulate all these hon. members on their remarks. He was greatly concerned about the fisheries in New Brunswick, and in his own county of Gloucester in particular. He spoke of the great need of public works, but did not in any way compliment this government on its budget or upon what it was doing for his part of the country.
Yesterday I listened to the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Michaud). He spoke of the great difficulties being experienced by the farmers of Kent county, and of the fact there are no markets for our fisheries. He spoke about the people leaving the county of Kent. He could have gone further and spoken about the people who are leaving the province of New Brunswick and the maritime provinces. He said that only the old and very young people were left in his constituency. He mentioned the fact that the old people were receiving the old age pension and the very young were receiving family allowances. The young men who wish to start homes, the people we are anxious to keep in the mari-times, unfortunately are the ones who are leaving.
I could go on and mention the remarks of other hon. members, such as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Lusby). I wish also to congratulate him on his speech. It was a well prepared address, and he had a strong feeling for his own county of Cumberland as well as for the rest of Nova Scotia. His complaint was, as was the complaint of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, concerned with the sad situation of the coal industry in Nova Scotia today. As I say, there was little in any of these speeches that I feel would commend this budget that has been introduced to the people of the maritime provinces.
I cannot say that I was altogether disappointed in the budget. I have been in this house now for quite a number of years, and I have learned from experience that a postelection budget is never a very satisfactory budget so far as the people are concerned. We have learned not to expect very much, and we were not disappointed in the budget in that respect this year. Some reductions in taxes were made, but as has been pointed out by numerous speakers they were mostly on luxury goods. So far as my home town of Sussex is concerned, I was pleased to note there would be a reduction in the excise tax on soft drinks. There are two manufacturers of soft drinks in the town of Sussex, and this reduction will be of benefit to them.

I was not so well pleased, Mr. Speaker, with the resolution that proposes to tax mutual insurance companies. Resolution No. 6 of the budget resolutions proposes this tax on mutual insurance companies doing business in all parts of Canada. In New Brunswick we have five small mutual insurance companies and, as everyone knows, they are made up mostly of farmers. In the 1930's it was very difficult for the farmers to obtain fire insurance. They banded together and formed these companies in order to help themselves. As far as these companies are concerned the government now proposes to tax what is known as underwriting gains. In some years, over and above the amount of money which is collected from the premiums, there are certain gains. In other years, naturally there are losses. It depends on the amount of money that has to be paid out for fire losses. I understand that these companies are not objecting to any tax assessment on the interest of their earnings, and that is very important; but they do object to a tax on the underwriting gains of the company. The matter came before the Supreme Court of Canada. I might say that the company which was responsible for bringing this matter before the Supreme Court of Canada was the Stanley Mutual Insurance Company of Stanley, New Brunswick. It is one of the five small companies of this kind that we have in the province.
The judgment of Mr. Justice Locke of the Supreme Court of Canada, which was concurred in by the other five judges who sat on the appeal bench, was that these companies should not be taxed. They declared that the gains were not profits. I should like to read just what Mr. Justice Locke said:
"The question is whether the surplus resulting from the amounts received from premiums paid in cash at the time the insurance is effected and from assessments being in excess of that required for the company's operation is a profit or a gain" . . . "no question arises regarding the interest earned upon the company's investment of its reserve fund which is conceded to be taxable."
The court held that the underwriting gain of a mutual was neither profit nor gain so as to be taxable within the terms of the Income Tax Act.
I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to labour this point further; but I feel that, taking into consideration the judgment of the supreme court and taking into consideration the fact that these companies, as I know them at least, are small companies which are banded together in order to assist farmers mostly, in all fairness this resolution should be withdrawn and there should be no tax

imposed as far as these companies are concerned. I hope that resolution No. 6 will be withdrawn.
The minister was very optimistic in his budget. I feel that very few share his optimism when he said as reported at page 3726 of Hansard:
My reasons for saying this are, first, that the support to be given to production in 1954 in the principal areas where demand originates is well assured. This statement holds good whether we look at the intentions of Canadian business with respect to new investment, or at the probable expenditures of Canadians as consumers or builders of new houses, or at the rate of government expenditures, or at the prospects for export.
As far as business investment intentions are concerned, in 1953 the business investment was $5,059 million. As far as the proposal for 1954 is concerned, it is -4 per cent lower than it was in 1953, which does not indicate that business expects to improve. The minister has told us that there would be an upward swing in the second half of 1954. Well, it is May of 1954, and we shall not have to wait very long to see whether there is an upward swing. I may say that there are very few indications of it at the present time. Unemployment is not only increasing-

Yes; fifty-fifty. When we
discuss a provincial-dominion conference I feel that this is one of the first subjects which should be discussed at such a conference. No matter what some members may think, I have a feeling that there is fairness among all the members from all parts of Canada. I know it has often been said that we do a great deal of complaining in the maritime provinces. May I say that we have had a great deal to complain about. We are sometimes told to help ourselves. That is always good advice, not only for provinces but for individuals. We in New Brunswick feel that we can help ourselves. We have always been considered to be one of the poorer provinces but, as hon. members know, in recent years we have been fortunate to discover in our province minerals which, in the past, we did not know we had.
We are told that one of the great reasons why we have not developed more industry is that we have not cheap electric power. In order to develop our mineral resources, to attract industry and to develop more industry we must have cheap electric power. The government of New Brunswick have been trying to solve this problem, as have past governments in that province. Today they think they have a solution in the development of more power on the Saint John river by means of a project called the Beechwood project. It is a project which, for full development, will cost a considerable sum of


money; it will cost more than the province of New Brunswick can afford. For a partial development, which is being promoted at the present time, the cost will be about $44 million. The development of this hydroelectric power will mean a great deal to the province of New Brunswick. It will probably mean the difference between prosperity and difficult times.
1 understand that the government of New Brunswick have approached the federal government, not to ask them to develop the Beechwood project but to ask them for assistance in raising money for the development of hydroelectric power at Beechwood. They have asked the assistance of the federal government by way of making available treasury loans so that they might have a lower nominal rate of interest than they would have if the province of New Brunswick is obliged to borrow the money from outside sources. I do not know what the attitude of the federal government is to this proposition but I think that the proposition that has been made to the federal government is a very fair one. It is one which will mean a great deal to New Brunswick and I hope it will be accepted. It is not one that is going to increase the debt of the dominion. It is not going to mean that the people in other parts of Canada will have to give one cent. The province of New Brunswick will pay its debts. But with the backing of the federal government it can raise money at lower rates of interest than would otherwise be possible, thus making hydroelectric power available to the people of New Brunswick more cheaply than would otherwise be possible. As I say, I hope that this matter will receive serious consideration by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to sit out this discussion but, as it goes on and on, I feel that I might as well make my contribution also. I first want to compliment the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Buchanan) on his maiden speech. Having regard to the fact that he is a new member, that we have a complicated budget and that we are living in twisted times, I thought that he took a rather realistic view of the whole situation. He did an excellent job. As his next-door neighbour on Cape Breton island I feel it to be my duty to say that I am extremely pleased with his attitude, his manner and his general approach to this problem of the budget. However, Mr. Speaker, I cannot say that I can pay that tribute to every hon. member to whose speech I have listened.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria said that, having regard to the times in which we are living, this year was

a good time to take a look around. I think that anyone who is doing any reading at the present time will have to come to that conclusion. I think he will be forced to the conclusion that we are not just faced with a temporary recession and that it is not something that is going to cure itself. The whole thing arises out of faulty mechanics in society. The situation in which we find ourselves indicates that we did not learn much from the last war. In my judgment present circumstances indicate that we are headed back for what we had in 1939 unless some down-to-earth, realistic thinking is done by those in charge of the management of the economy of, not only Canada but of the United States.
I have here in my hand a copy of a magazine called The Reporter. It is a United States publication and it is a rather exclusive one. Some fairly good writers contribute to it. The issue I have in my hand is that of March 30, 1954. In it there is an article with the caption "The Recession is Here". It is written by an economist who takes a look at the whole economy of the United States. He runs through, industry by industry, the present inventories, the percentage of drop-offs, the general market trends and all that kind of thing. The conclusion at which he arrives is that as far as the United States is concerned the recession is here. I am not going to read that article because I like to read these things for myself and to summarize them. Anyone who is interested can pick up the magazine and read it for himself. I consider that article to be an authoritative one written by a man who is not grinding any axe. He is merely reading the danger signs as they affect the economy of the United States.
I think anybody who is reading the newspapers will have to agree with me. What is true of the United States is also true of Canada because the economy of this country is so tightly locked to the economy of the United States that anything that happens over there will spill over into Canada. I am sure that any member of the house who takes a look at our basic industries today must agree that basic changes have got to be made. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) missed coal and steel but he did talk about the textile and electrical industries and the difficulties that are facing agriculture.
We have heard discussion about picayune savings in government expenditures, but I do not think they would have very much effect. Someone says that you can cut off a few civil servants, stop publishing certain books and save a million and a half dollars. That kind of thing is unrealistic in the type of situation that confronts us today. I have

The Budget-Mr. Gillis able to get up in the house and put his finger on some place where there is inefficiency, then in my judgment the saving of money is not argument enough in the circumstances that this country faces today. The more purchasing power in circulation the greater the chances are of avoiding unemployment, which is our big problem at the present time.
I heard a member who sits not very far from me suggest that the construction of the new C.N.R. hotel in Montreal was a terrible thing and should not be undertaken at this time, that it was going to cost $20 million and someone was going to have to pay for it. I heard that matter discussed in the railway committee. The construction of that building in the city of Montreal is necessary. Before the committee the president of the C.N.R. pointed out the fact that in the city of Montreal there is not a hotel with accommodation for the type of conventions that take place today in Canada where 600, 800,
1,000	or 1,500 delegates assemble. He is quite right because I have had the experience of attending one or two conventions where the convention had to be divided, and that does not tend to good business.
The president of the C.N.R. also pointed out that he has applications from organizations all over the United States that will mean that the hotel will be booked solid with conventions for at least two years after it is completed. The project will pay for itself. It is a self-liquidating project. Some people talk as though Canada were through developing. They talk as though we did not need any more population and give the impression that we should just sit tight, put our money in the sock and all that kind of thing. This country is developing and the hotel project in Montreal will help to solve the unemployment problem to some extent in that city.
I heard a lot of other proposals along the same line, but as far as I am concerned not one of them would stand up. In my judgment they do not mean anything.

This afternoon I listened with a great deal of interest to the Leader of the Opposition. His speech was my principal reason for rising at this time because he dealt with a subject that is extremely important to the end of the country from which I come, the subject of dominion-provincial agreements. When he referred to unemployment and so forth, whether or not he realized it, he made one of the best cases against the so-called system of free enterprise that I ever heard. In effect what he said about marketing and the breakdown as it were of the whole set-up proved conclusively the inability of industry in this country to compete today. We had a similar situation on our hands from the twenties to 1939 when we got into another war and, to a certain extent, our economy was planned. Then our economy worked well, and even though we were throwing away 50 per cent of our national income there was prosperity and full employment.

When the shooting was over the government removed the controls and returned control to General Motors, Dominion Steel and Coal, Canada Packers, General Electric and the rest of them. Before the trenches were filled in they were sitting back uttering the same old cry; there is unemployment, and we cannot compete. That is the picture the Leader of the Opposition painted this afternoon. I believe he was quite right in the figures he presented. There is no purpose served by the Minister of Labour or anyone else trying to rationalize the question of unemployment. Figures presented by the minister in this house a month or so ago showed that there were about
520.000	unemployed. He told us also that about 56,000 people who were receiving unemployment insurance would not receive any benefits after April 21.
Now, perhaps the Leader of the Opposition brought the figures up to date when he said that according to information he had there were 570,000 on the unemployment insurance rolls. He said that actually there were
730.000	people looking for work. If this latter figure is correct, I would say that there are about 270,000 people in this country who have been removed from the unemployment insurance rolls and therefore have no income. I know that in my own area there were about 1,100 who were removed from the unemployment insurance rolls on April 21. These people have no income at all. Something has to be done about that. My recommendation is not that the government should fire a few civil servants somewhere or cut out a publication; that is not going to solve the problem. Something has to be done immediately.
My suggestion is, and has been, that unemployment insurance benefits should be extended. They should be extended until such time as these people can be put to work. If the government has to subsidize this fund, then that is too bad but people have the right to eat; that is a prior right.
There is another thought I should like to leave with the minister. One hears it everywhere because I think everyone has picked it up today as their swan song. We are told we have priced ourselves out of the market. Wage rates in Canada are too high. There is another side to that story. Perhaps profits in Canada are too high also. If one looks at some of the recent balance sheets published in the press one finds that profits are very high. Before the captains of industry in Canada start telling the workers that $2 or $1.60 an hour is too high, they should look at their own rates. An example should be set.
I have in my hand a paper called The Guardian, which is the official organ of local 195 of the auto workers union. This little
The Budget-Mr. Gillis paper does a good research job. In talking about wages, the Minister of Labour should remember this. General Motors has quite an unemployment problem, both in United States and in Canada. According to this paper the president of General Motors, in 1953, had an income of $637,233; that is a lot of money. It is $368 an hour for the forty-hour week or $6 a minute. I am leaving this thought with the Minister of Labour because he will be meeting delegations of these people who will tell him they cannot compete with Britain; they cannot compete with the mass production methods of the United States, and their only solution will be to pull down the standard of living in Canada by reducing wage rates. Before that argument presented by the top executives in Canada becomes valid, they should start to make readjustments in their own house. I have just given one example of the amount of money that is paid to those who feel the worker who produces that wealth should take a cut every time they get into trouble. I mention that to the minister because I have heard a lot about it recently, and I know he has. It has all come from the same people, the people who are in the $368 an hour bracket. They should put their own house in order first.
Let me say a few words on this question of dominion-provincial agreements. I do not want to pose as an authority on the British North America Act. I want to say that so long as you have the centralization of wealth in Canada, such as you have in Ontario and Quebec, and a centralization of industry that keeps in the two central provinces about 80 per cent of the wealth of Canada, there is no other way by which you can get any amount of equality for the rest of Canada except by having the taxing powers in the hands of the federal government. Then, as the member for Cape Breton North and Victoria said, the federal government can redistribute some of that wealth to the hewers of wood and drawers of water on the prairies and in the maritimes.
I knew this was going to be a pertinent question, so before I went home for Easter I took a look at some of the figures for my own province. I wanted to see where we would be without these dominion-provincial agreements. The argument has been advanced that the provinces are losing something. For twenty years before coming into this house I listened to talk about the amalgamation of corporations being good business. By an amalgamation of corporations across the country and the head offices in the centre of Canada you cut your administrative costs 100 per cent as far as management is concerned, and it is good business. That is what has been going on. We have been taking from
4398	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gillis the outlying provinces most of their wealth and putting it into the two central provinces. The taxes are paid there; the succession duties are paid there and so forth.
I know that Nova Scotia was reluctant to come into these dominion-provincial agreements. There are a lot of people in this country who, when you give them a little job and a little bit of authority, insist on holding that, even if it is just presiding over the poverty that exists in the area. I never could get it myself. It is true that Nova Scotia did not want to come into these agreements but our provincial budget this year will be around $48 million. Some $23 million to $25 million of that money will come back under these dominion-provincial agreements. In personal and corporation income taxes we will pay to the federal government around $30 million; but what are we getting back? That is the point. The fact that this dominion-provincial agreement existed is the only reason that we are getting it back.
I took a look at the family allowance payments in that province from 1946 to 1954, during the lifetime of these agreements, and I found that during that period $131,499 280 was paid in family allowances alone in the province of Nova Scotia since the establishment of the dominion-provincial agreements. In the matter of old age security $39,083,367 has been paid. We have received that amount in these two items alone. Then we come to old age assistance, and during that time the federal government has contributed to old age assistance $1,988,733. In the matter of blind allowances, in the three-year period we have received $617,917 in that field alone. From 1947 to 1953 the subventions on the movement of coal amounted to $5,949,000 odd, or $2.40 a ton on the 2,405,767 tons of coal moved during that period.
For vocational assistance in the establishment of schools in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, certain amounts were paid by the federal government to the provinces. During that year $63 900.59 went to Nova Scotia. I have the figures for the other provinces but they are not relevant to my discussion. Hon. members can see from that that if it was not for these dominion-provincial agreements where we would fit in that province, and that is equally true of New Brunswick, or much more so, and it is equally true of the prairie provinces, and partially true of British Columbia.
As long as my hon. friends who oppose these dominion-provincial agreements are prepared to maintain the kind of centralization of industry and wealth in these two provinces of Canada that exists, in order for the other provinces to exist there has to be some


method of redistributing the wealth of this country in the way that it is now done by the federal government.
The Leader of the Opposition brought up the example of Ontario and their 7 per cent. That is true, but it was done by agreement. As I see the present proposal, it was not done by agreement. The province of Quebec enacted the 15 per cent tax, and after they enacted it they said they wanted it to be used as an offset to the federal tax. Well, that is not agreement. The other nine provinces of this country cannot be wrong. Everybody is not out of step except Duplessis, I hope, in this matter of redistributing the wealth of this country. As one member of this house who lives in a section of Canada that likes to be called Canadian, I am glad that the federal government have taken the position that they are going to maintain the kind of policy in taxation that means the greatest good to the greatest number of Canadians. And as I indicated a moment ago, it is in the best interests of the great majority of the people of this country that these dominion-provincial taxation agreements should be maintained.
I do not say they are perfect, but they are a start, and they are subject to discussion and reason from time to time. I would not see any difficulty in the dominion-provincial agreements, as far as Quebec is concerned, if someone came in, sat down and talked the matter over. That is democracy. The right to agree and to disagree and intelligent compromise will be the final result that is democracy. Anyone who is not prepared to do that is not prepared to accept the mechanics of democracy.
I will join with the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, and say that anything that I can do as an individual member to see that a system whereby we can at least get something back from the centre is maintained, as it is in the dominion-provincial agreements, I will do. [DOT]
People should realize that the wealth of industry that they have in the central provinces was taken from the provinces east and west. We lost fifty industries in the province of Nova Scotia in fewer than fifty years, and a lot of them were large industries, to Quebec and Ontario. Most of the high salaries paid in steel and coal in these organizations today, and the dividends, go to Mount Royal in Montreal, and the taxes are paid in the province of Quebec. The only method that I know of whereby we can at least get some payments to enable us to stay in the field of social security is by redistributing the wealth in the way that we are doing at the present time. But the time will come when we will realize that industry in

this country has to be decentralized to a greater extent than it is at the present time.
In summing up the Leader of the Opposition mentioned what the premier of Ontario had to say in regard to the signing of the agreement. He told me at least that what the premier of Ontario was complaining about was the burden imposed on municipalities and service organizations in this province by the indiscriminate laying down in Ontario of industry after industry that they are not prepared to cater to. First, they developed a huge power shortage. It has made it necessary to develop the Niagara falls project. They went around half in darkness during the war to conserve power because of the great centralization of industry in this province of Ontario.
I notice that in the United States today they are being advised by experts to get busy and to start to decentralize their industrial machine in that country, both for economic reasons and as a greater measure of protection in the event of war.
You know, it is a strange thing but the only reports from any corporations I have seen recently that seem to indicate they are getting along all right are the reports from government-owned plants. Everyone else is screaming. Canada's publicly-owned rubber factory, it is pointed out, is a profitable success. I do not need to read what is said about it. But I do say that the government is going to have to make changes along the lines represented by Trans-Canada Air Lines, the Polymer Corporation and Canadian Arsenals, because these organizations are planning their production. Others are not. It is this type of planned organization which must be implemented in the future if we are going to meet competition from outside. We will have to sit down together and realize that not just a few people own Canada but all the people of Canada are shareholders in the future of our country. If adjustments are necessary, then we can make them together.
But I do say it is bad taste for someone who is receiving $6 a minute to tell someone else that he should work for less than $1.60 an hour. That kind of thing is going to bring about what happened in Europe. It will drag the house of cards down around our ears.
I should like to say a word to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) concerning the unemployment figures we have today. Every second paper one reads contains a story about an increase in immigration. I have here a small clipping which says that 25,000 families are to be admitted to Canada. At one point in Ontario the minister made a statement a couple of
The Budget-Mr. Gillis months ago that we are going to bring
186,000	immigrants into Canada this year. Well, I would say to him that this is a bad year to be thinking along those lines. As I have said on many occasions in the house, our immigration program lacks planning. No one seems to be taking a look at industry, or at the problems of agriculture, and determining the kind of people we should bring into this country, whether there are homes for them or jobs they can fill. In other words no one seems to be considering the contribution these people must be prepared to make to Canada.
This would be a good time to stop and take a look around. When one looks into this question of immigration he finds that people are saying, "Yes, but there is the humanitarian reason to be considered." Of course there is; I admit that. But let us understand the situation. If we are going to take in 186,000 persons for humanitarian reasons let us be prepared to tax ourselves to feed them. It is not good enough to take them in and drop them in centres already overcrowded so that they will be bidding for jobs against people who have jobs, or for homes when there are no homes available. That is not good enough. If we are taking them in for humanitarian reasons, then let us understand that that is so. But our centres are overcrowded today. The cities in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia are badly overcrowded. I would strongly urge the Minister of Labour that the first thing that must be done is to put those unemployed persons who have gone off the relief rolls in a position where at least they will be able to take something home to eat.
Until we get around to a point of ironing out the problems of competition we are up against, this fact must be considered. It will not be easy, because the average industrialist wants to make money. If he can take an industry from Canada and transfer it to Africa or Japan or China, or some other country in which he can get cheap labour, and then sell his products in this country, he will do so. It has been done before, and to some extent it is happening today.
We have a serious problem on our hands. So far as my approach to the budget is concerned, I would say it is not a political approach, because my first concern is for the country at large. I am not unmindful of the fact that in two wars thousands upon thousands of our young people offered their lives to see that this country remained fit to live in, and so that we might maintain our institutions as we have them. I would not want to quibble about anything that was good for this country, because I want to see it prosperous.

The Budget-Mr. Cardin
Having said that, let me add that I notice from the press that our genial Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) has been invited to become the skipper of the ship in Nova Scotia. If I had a vote on that, I would vote for it because something is wrong in that province. It needs a good captain at the present time. There is nothing wrong in the province that could not be cured by a little bit of common sense and some honesty. That is one of the things badly needed in public affairs, generally, of this country-a little honesty.
Whether the Hon. Bob Winters is going to Nova Scotia or not remains to be seen. But I would say that under prevailing conditions in the province-steel production is down; 1,700 men have been laid off from the steel plant; we know that the coal industry is in a bad way-I know from my visits there that they are looking around to see what can be done. Of course it is a job for the Liberal party. As I said before, however, I am interested in the welfare of Nova Scotia and of Canada. I am also interested in seeing that anyone who is calling the shots in any section of the country should have some realistic approach, as well as the courage and the necessary honesty to do that which is right rather than that which is politically exDedient. I am not going to give the minister any advice; but I do hope Bob Winters will go back down to Nova Scotia. I believe he could make a valuable contribution down there; and I know the people of that province well enough to know this that, despite politics, any approach he would make to the problems of the province would meet with co-operation and assistance, because the people down there want to have something done.
These remarks have been rambling, I realize. My main reason in rising was to make some observations on the dominion-provincial agreements. In my view they represent a long step forward and mean a great deal to the provinces outside of Quebec and Ontario It means that some of the wealth siphoned off from those provinces can be returned by way of social security payments, as they are at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years and particularly during these past few months an unfortunate propaganda campaign has been conducted in the province of Quebec to convince the population that the federal government is not only alien to Quebec but moreover hostile towards that province, and that federal legislation aims at nothing but the destruction of


the autonomy of Quebec, and the violation of the rights and privileges granted to it by the constitution of the country.
It seems to me, however, that it is only since confederation, since the establishment of a central government that the government of Quebec, the province of Quebec and its population have been able to exercise fully their rights and their freedom. It is also since confederation that the province of Quebec has made tremendous strides in every field, so that it is now one of the greatest and one of the most prosperous in Canada.
It is also since the central government exists that the French Canadians have been able to play with the other citizens of Canada their rightful part in the administration of this country.
There is no need, Mr. Speaker, to spend much time looking through the history book or the pages of daily papers to find the names of French Canadians who have been and are still standing guard over the destinies of the province of Quebec, as well as over the destinies of this country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, we have had, in the province of Quebec, to find a solution to many difficult questions and thorny problems, but they are now things of the past, and the province of Quebec never lost any of her constitutional rights, and the problem which now besets my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec will go down in history without the position of the province of Quebec undergoing any change whatsoever. Our province will always remain the place where our children will have the freedom and the right to speak the tongue and practise the religion of their forefathers.
There is not one Liberal member from the province of Quebec who would support the government if he thought that our autonomy, our race or our religion were endangered in the slightest degree by the legislation of the present government. We too are French Canadians and we want, as well as anyone else, to keep our language, our rights and our religion, but we would not be justified, for example, in indulging in unwarranted demagogy and sentimentalism, which would be detrimental rather than helpful to the people of the province of Quebec.
When our forefathers decided to establish a confederation, they did so because they saw certain advantages in that set-up and today all the Canadian provinces benefit from social and economic advantages which only confederation can give to each of the provinces. But the advantages also entailed

certain obligations, among them those upon which rests the very constitution of Canada, that is co-operation and understanding between the provincial governments and the central government, without which there can be no confederation, there can be no national unity, there cannot be any nation.
Mr. Speaker, for the people of the province of Quebec, provincial autonomy is extremely precious and sacred, but we should never lose sight of the fact that national unity is also very important. It is only through sincere co-operation between the governments of the provinces and the central government that Canada can take its place among the great nations of the world in order to settle and direct international affairs and at the same time look after the defence, the economy and the social security of each of the provinces that make up Canada.
I believe that we, of the province of Quebec, should be proud that our nation, which was born on the very soil of the province of Quebec, has become in a few short years, a strong, free and sovereign country, as was envisioned by the fathers of confederation.
Mr. Speaker, I believe we should show the same eagerness to safeguard national unity as we have shown to preserve and safeguard provincial autonomy, because as long as the province of Quebec is part and parcel of confederation, its welfare and its interests wiii be closely related to those of the government of Canada.
Protection of national unity is not tantamount to betrayal of the autonomy of the province of Quebec. These are not incompatible. That idea was well expressed in this house by one whose love for and devotion to the province of Quebec could certainly not be doubted.
I would like to quote in this connection the words spoken by the Hon. P. J. A. Cardin in this house, on November 30, 1944:
In the evening of my life, from the point of view of age and of parliamentary service, let me through you, Mr. Speaker, and from my place in the House of Commons, address just a word to the citizens of the province of Quebec and ask them, whatever may be their sentiments, whatever be their feelings at the present time, to take things easy, to reflect before acting, and to remember that they are not only citizens of the province of Quebec but at the same time citizens of Canada as a whole, who desire to see their country in the not distant future, and with the will of all concerned, become a great and independent country.
They are as much interested as I am, as much interested as others are in the future of our great land, and they should do all they can to help to build up, on the foundation of confederation, a great and prosperous country, which, with the help of God and the concerted effort of those who are
The Budget-Mr. Cardin
in authority, before long will be a country of which we shall be proud and in which we shall have great honour.
Mr. Speaker, those words apply equally to the present situation. They are as true as they were in 1944, and I submit it would be unworthy on the part of the province of Quebec to want to share in the benefits of confederation without recognizing the heavy responsibilities of the federal government and to deny its co-operation in the solution of an extremely complicated problem which concerns every province in Canada.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the stand taken by the premier of the province of Quebec can surely be interpreted as being un-cooperative; in fact it has even been aggressive in some instances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose, I was saying that it was unfortunate that the attitude of the prime minister of Quebec showed a lack of co-operation and was even, at times, aggressive. In some Quebec circles, the idea seems to prevail that it is still possible to change Quebec into a sovereign state. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that one would have to be very shortsighted to wish to secede from our confederation at a time such as the present when all the countries of the world are grouping themselves together in order to repulse the attack of the enemy if it comes and to protect more efficiently their national economy.
All the unrest and the misunderstandings now present in Quebec seem to revolve around the claim made by the premier of Quebec that federal-provincial agreements are directly opposed to provincial autonomy and aim solely at the destruction of the French-Canadian element.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is difficult to justify such accusations because federal-provincial agreements are legal contracts which must and shall be upheld before all courts of justice, especially since the preamble of each of those agreements contains a paragraph which formally guarantees the constitutional rights of the provinces and of the central government. I would like once again, Mr. Speaker, to quote the preamble of the agreements signed between the Cana-

The Budget-Mr. Cardin dian government and that of the province of Ontario. In fact I believe the preamble throws so much light on this whole problem of provincial autonomy, that I took the trouble of translating it into French. I now quote the preamble of the agreements between the province of Ontario and the Canadian government:
Whereas, in view of the desire of the parties hereto to avoid as far as practicable a dual system of direct taxation, the parties hereto have resolved to enter into an agreement designed (a) to establish a more equitable system of taxation throughout Canada by reducing duplication of direct taxation and of machinery for the collection of direct taxes, (b) to give a greater measure of stability to the revenue of the province in order to enable it more adequately to carry out its responsibilities, and (c) to enable Canada, with the co-operation of provincial governments, to carry out fiscal and other national policies intended to maintain high levels of employment and production;
And whereas it is agreed that neither Canada nor the province shall be deemed by reason of having entered into this agreement to have surrendered, abandoned or given over to the other any of the powers, rights, privileges or authorities vested in it under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, and any amendments thereto, or otherwise, or to have impaired any of such powers, rights, privileges or authorities;
Mr. Speaker, may I point out here that the agreements offered to the province of Quebec were drafted in exactly the same terms.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it would seem difficult to entertain any opinion unfavourable to federal-provincial agreements, if we consider, besides, that these agreements are only to operate for five years and that they are after all only temporary measures made necessary by an urgent problem, as much in the interest of the province of Quebec as in that of Canada as a whole. It is also difficult to understand, Mr. Speaker, why such agreements could have been termed injurious to the autonomy of the provinces, or again why it was thought necessary to refuse benefits accruing from them, since all other provinces in Canada have benefited thereby.
I do not intend to repeat the constitutional and fiscal arguments which were brilliantly set forth by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) and by the hon. members for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard), Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton), Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) and Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault). They proved beyond the shadow of a doubt


that the federal government had a right equal to that of the province of Quebec to levy a direct tax and that moreover the dominion-provincial agreements brought financial benefits to the province of Quebec.
It would be useless to try to add anything to the brief and lucid statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in this house yesterday afternoon, when he showed the only stand the federal government could adopt under the circumstances. It would also be useless for me to try to open the doors wider to welcome the province of Quebec than did the right hon. the Prime Minister in order to find a solution which would provide relief for the taxpayers in the province of Quebec.
In spite of the logic of his argument based on rights as much as on facts, the premier of Quebec does not seem to want to understand the position and goes on repeating false accusations to the effect that the federal government wishes to annihilate French Canadians. Well, Mr. Speaker, while this dispute is continuing between the two governments, Quebec taxpayers, who pay more provincial taxes than any other Canadian citizens, must, moreover, unfairly and uselessly bear double taxation caused by the recent introduction of a provincial tax in Quebec. It seems to me that, under the circumstances, the parties involved should consider first and foremost some relief for the Quebec taxpayers and then solve their problem with the calmness, peace and levelheadedness that are necessary for the settlement of such an important constitutional issue.
It might perhaps be well, Mr. Speaker, if I briefly recapitulated the facts that have brought about the present situation in the province of Quebec.
1.	The country faces a financial problem which no magic formula can solve.
2.	Agreements have been proposed to solve that problem and enable the federal government to honour its obligations.
3.	When those proposals were made to the provinces, it was understood that if one or more provinces did not wish to sign such agreements, and insisted upon collecting directly from the taxpayers, these taxpayers could deduct 5 per cent of the tax they were supposed to pay to the federal government.

4.	The Quebec premier refused to sign such agreements, claiming that they constituted an attack against autonomy. He even refused to take advantage of that 5 per cent deduction, which gave him the right to collect a 5 per cent tax, which since 1948 would have represented $53 million.
5.	The premier of Quebec, without consulting the federal government and without any notice whatsoever, imposed a 15 per cent tax on the income of Quebec taxpayers.
6.	Once such a tax was established, he asked the federal government to deduct all of that 15 per cent.
The federal government had to refuse the authorization to deduct that 15 per cent tax in the interest of national unity because when the agreements were signed with the other provinces of Canada, it was understood that the taxpayers of provinces that did not sign would be able to deduct 5 per cent of the tax paid to their provincial government. If the federal government had granted the authorization to deduct that 15 per cent tax, the provinces that signed the agreements under those conditions could have protested against such a violation of the terms of the contract. They could have abandoned the agreements and the federal government would have been faced with the same problem that existed prior to the agreements.
Moreover, in doing so the federal government would have endangered national unity in Canada.
In listening to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) this afternoon, I asked myself whether he was considering that national unity was not a good enough reason to justify the government's attitude in refusing to authorize a deduction greater than 5 per cent, before the federal-provincial agreements signed between the federal government and the nine other Canadian provinces come to an end. I also wondered whether the Leader of the Opposition, if he were responsible for the administration of this country, would have, under these circumstances, taken upon himself to grant a deduction of more than 5 per cent to the province of Quebec.
As things are, and after seriously considering the situation, the federal government could do nothing but refuse the 15 per cent deductibility requested by the government of the province of Quebec. As the tax had
The Budget-Mr. Cardin already been put into force by the premier of that province, Quebec taxpayers found themselves squeezed between double taxation, without the federal government being able to do anything to help them.
Reviewing those facts, it might be possible to bring redress to the taxpayers who were wronged by the premier of the province of Quebec. Apparently, that 15 per cent tax levied on the personal income of the Quebec taxpayers was intended to yield the amounts needed for health and education, and they claim that the province will derive from that source an additional revenue of approximately $22 million. One can estimate that within three years the province of Quebec will have thus collected about $66 million.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I suggest there could be an agreement if, on the one hand, the Quebec government were to offer to suspend its new income tax legislation, which it has introduced for a period of three years, that is until 1957, and if, as compensation, the federal government were, upon being formally authorized to do so by the Quebec taxpayers, to grant to that province $53 million, i.e. the amount which could have been deducted from what has been levied from these taxpayers in federal income tax and that the Quebec government could have collected had it imposed a 5 per cent income tax back in 1948.
The provincial government could then, for a period of three years, impose a 5 per cent tax, according to the provisions of the federal income tax legislation, as well as to the terms of the agreements. This would bring to the provincial treasury $14 million. In this way, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec would have collected approximately $95 million, that is $29 million more than it would collect by imposing this double taxation.
In that manner the federal government would have respected the spirit and the letter of the terms of the agreements signed with the other provinces.
When the agreements with the other provinces come to an end in 1957, the Quebec government and those of the other provinces of Canada will then be in a position to try to find a permanent solution to the problem we are confronted with today, and that, in the light of the conditions and circumstances then prevailing.
Perhaps I do not see the objections or arguments one can raise against my suggestion, but it seems to me you find there at least the

The Budget-Mr. Cardin basis for an honourable compromise which could be accepted by the Quebec government, nor does my suggestion jeopardize national unity and, after all, would afford relief to the taxpayers in the province of Quebec by delivering them of this burden of double taxation. However I cannot help repeating here that such a compromise is much more complicated and still much less advantageous than the signing of the federal-provincial agreements themselves, which do not violate, either, any part of the rights or autonomy of the province of Quebec.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, 1 shall be accused of betraying my province, my faith and my people. It will be implied that I do not understand the unique position of the province of Quebec within Canada. Some are going to pretend that I do not cherish our autonomy, our faith, or our language as much as our opponents do, but I am satisfied, absolutely satisfied, that it is not by introducing double taxation in the province of Quebec that we shall be able to help our fellow citizens. Neither is it by placing our Quebec industries at a disadvantage that we shall be able to assist the people of Quebec. The refusal to refund 3 per cent interest to those who want to avail themselves of our federal housing legislation will not help our fellow citizens in Quebec to become home owners. It is not by refusing millions of dollars, through hostility to all federal legislation, while weakening the economy of the province of Quebec and posing as a martyr that the premier of Quebec will best serve the people of his province. On the contrary, if our economy is sound and stable, our universities, our technical schools, our colleges, our primary and secondary schools will be in a position not only to survive but also to dispense their science and teaching to a greater number of our young people who, in turn, will take care of the rights, privileges and traditions bequeathed to us by our forefathers.
No, I am neither afraid nor ashamed to uphold the federal-provincial agreements which are neither more nor less than temporary means of getting around a serious and complicated problem and that with a view fully to protecting our national unity.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the premier of the province of Quebec does not want to sign the agreements, if he does not accept the proposals made here or any other proposals, I

hope, in all sincerity, that he will be kind enough, for the sake of the Quebec taxpayers, to offer some alternative to the federal government.
For I am convinced that there is for the province of Quebec a way of escape from the present deadlock in which she finds herself provided that Mr. Duplessis really wants to show his desire to co-operate with the federal government, a desire about which he spoke at such length at federal-provincial conferences.

Mr. John Pallet! (Peel): Mr. Speaker, I wish to say at the outset I consider it a very real privilege to be allowed to sit in this house in company with some of the greatest statesmen of our time. I regret, as does this whole house, the untimely death of Gordon Graydon which necessitated the by-election which preceded my taking this seat. It is my earnest desire to give my country the same high quality of service that was given by the former member for Peel. It is a privilege extended to few Canadians and, attendant with that privilege, are heavy responsibilities.
It would be remiss of me if I did not on this occasion commend to this house certain matters, and one in particular of great national interest. It seems to me that being one of the newest members of the house I can speak perhaps more as a layman than as a house expert. I, personally, am satisfied that my remarks carry the complete support of my county and I am satisfied they will carry the support of the majority of the people of this country.
Some governments have a political philosophy to the effect that rather than introduce legislation that is farsighted and visionary, or shall we say anticipatory, they would introduce legislation that is forced upon them and carries the momentum of the moment with it. They believe that a sounding of public opinion should first be taken, and on finding the legislation cannot be too dangerous to them politically it will be enacted. Tonight one of the matters that I would commend to your attention has the happy condition of containing both these elements of political philosophy, in that in many areas of Canada the momentum of the moment is behind it, while in other areas anyone taking the necessary steps would be blessed in the future with having been sufficiently farsighted to foretell the hardships which are presently occasioned in some parts of Canada.

We say, and with considerable pride, that nothing is too good for the young people of this country of ours. The government expounds the great advances we are making in our social services. The government expounds the great need to keep our ramparts strong in the military fashion against aggression. We say strongly that there must be equal opportunities for all. There is a situation that applies in Canada at the present time that will have the effect of making these platitudes sounded from a great height seem quite meagre and empty. Both by natural growth and by immigration for the past years the population of this country has been increasing considerably, which after all is a condition not unusual in any country after a war. I point out that the situation that must be dealt with tonight is one of the direct results of the increase in population.
Today across Canada the necessary expansion of school facilities is placing an uncompromising burden on the municipal taxpayer. In the long run this can only result in the curtailment of necessary educational services and the consequent reduction in the standard of education provided. This would indeed be a sorry thing in the lives of young Canadians, especially if the governments of the day stand by and do not seek some method by which our educational tradition can remain at a high level rather than be curtailed by austerity programs that are not in keeping with the other standards of living in this country.
I wish to make it plain that the solution of the educational problem must be arrived at without interfering in any way with the autonomous control of education enjoyed by the provinces. It may be argued that this
The Budget-Mr. Pallett educational problem is one which should be left to the provinces and not introduced on the floor of this house. On the contrary, today education is a national commodity. A person educated in Prince Edward Island may well work in the city of Toronto, and a person educated in the city of Toronto may well find employment in Victoria. The benefit of the education given in the formative years is enjoyed where the adult locates, and it is for that reason that I say there is a national interest in education. There is more than an interest merely in the standard of education. There is an interest also in the overwhelming burden the municipalities are being asked to share in the post-war expansion.
Everyone agrees that we must have more houses. With the development of more housing we find the demand on the municipalities for more services involving capital outlay. Some of the expenses incurred for these services, such as water and sewers, may be selfretiring in that the revenue will take care of the expenses incurred. However, there is no self-retiring basis for the expansion required in the educational field. Since the minister believes in a balanced budget and a retiring of the capital debt of the country, is it unreasonable to believe that the municipalities desire to do the same thing? It is evident that this philosophy cannot be carried out under the present system at the municipal level, except by curtailing necessary services.

It was admitted by the provinces and the municipalities that during the war years the federal budget required bumping up to meet the exigencies of the situation and, accordingly, certain concessions were given. It may be of interest to this house to know that without one increase in adult population in this country the educational costs will have doubled by the time the children now in grade 1 reach grade 8. In other words, educational costs in this country will have doubled without one increase in adult population in the next seven years.
I know it is not the intention of the members of this house that the educational systems of which we have become so proud shall be allowed, through lack of a few dollars, to become stagnant pools. We know it is the earnest desire of every member to see that the children in this country are properly educated. I believe that some hon. members are a little inclined to pooh-pooh the position of many of the municipalities, and I believe that a careful study by them of the municipal position will cause them to review their previous thoughts and will perhaps move them to take some concrete steps so that the municipalities which so gladly gave to this country when it was required during the war years will receive their just due at this time so they may continue with the proper services to their own residents.
If we accept the premise that there is a continued need for educational services, and if we accept the fact that the municipalities will shortly not be able to deal with it from their present sources of revenue, then the responsibility lies with this government to seek a satisfactory solution to the problem to ensure the future of the young Canada of today.

Mr. Speaker, I have deliberately refrained from quoting the fathers of confederation and those who have presided over the destinies of our country since then. I have much respect for those who drafted the constitution of 1867, but I believe that our present problem must be settled by our own statesmen, in the light of present conditions.
Owing to the enlightened patriotism of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), his sound judgment and foresight, I am confident that the problem that has arisen as a result of the new provincial income tax act will soon be settled.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to voice my opinion in this debate, but above all to plead the cause of the taxpayers of Lake St. John and of the province of Quebec as a whole.
The Saguenay-Lake St. John district has witnessed in recent years a truly extraordinary economic development as a result of its varied and numerous resources, and more particularly of its powerful hydraulic resources. The prosperous district of Chibougamau, which was a source of envy for the Abitibi and Lake St. John districts, can now be reached from either of them since the government has decided to build a railroad between St. Felicien and Chibougamau and from there to Beattyville.
The Liberal party, which was responsible for the industrial expansion of Lake St. John district in the past, deserves once again the gratitude of the whole Saguenay population for the sound decision which it has just taken, giving new impetus to such a stupendous development.
I would not like to resume my seat without extending special thanks to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The people of Lake St. John district want me to recognize, on their behalf, the part he played in bringing about this sound decision taken by the government.
Since I came here, I have advocated on three different occasions the construction of this railroad. Again last year, on March 2, 1953, it was my privilege to conduct and introduce a delegation from the Saguenay industrial development council to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier).
