speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my desire to take very much time in this debate. While I have not had the privilege of listening to many of the hon. members who have spoken, I have heard quite a few of them in the last few days and have found the speeches most interesting.
I do not think I would have taken part at all had it not been for a situation which seems to have been coming to a head in my own constituency, and apparently is reaching a point where it is serious. Most certainly I agree with other hon. members from the maritime provinces who have spoken. Invariably they have agreed that those of us in the maritimes do suffer disadvantages from which people in the rest of Canada do not seem to have to suffer. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has presented a rather prosperous picture in his budget. I imagine that almost everything has been said by way of general criticism, and also many speeches have been made supporting the minister's budget.
It would seem to me, from what I have read in Hansard and from what I have heard people say outside the House of Commons, that we appear to be running into a great deal of difficulty and, for such a prosperous country, there seem to be many trouble spots. We must realize that while there may be prosperity in some parts of the country there are many other places where there is a high degree of unemployment and where the people are having a difficult time. I think it is time this government along with others faced up to this situation. Before dealing with the subject about which I wish to speak I would like to quote a few words from the statement by the Minister of Finance as reported at page 3723 of Hansard where, referring I presume to the past year, he stated:
In the economic sphere, 1953 has been a much better year. Industrial and agricultural production in almost all countries has continued to expand, and consumption has risen.
Last Friday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said, as reported at page 4285 of Hansard:
I think, to state it mildly, that agriculture is in a better condition today throughout the Dominion of Canada than it has been at any other period in my experience. And when I say that, I do not mean only my experience in the government, but I mean as well my experience in farming. I think farmers all realize that they are in a better position today than they have been at any other time.
I am not disputing that from the government's standpoint in Ottawa and in studying
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery tables of statistics covering the entire country that might well be a fair statement to make, but each of us who sees the picture as it regards our own constituency arid the surrounding area has a very different perspective. We see the situation as it actually exists, and, as I pointed out before in this house, as it can be seen on the ground. From that point of view the government's outlook seems to be rather exaggerated, particularly when you compare their view with the situation as you know it and when you are familiar with the existing conditions.
Tonight I wish to spend a few minutes in dealing with the economy of my own constituency and the surrounding area in New Brunswick. The chief industry in that area happens to be potato farming. Very few people talk about potatoes in this house. I imagine there are other hon. members who could discuss this topic but most of them are on the government side of the house and I presume they are quite happy with the situation as they find it. However, I cannot say that for my own part because my people are not very happy at the moment. I believe the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and the Minister of Agriculture will agree with me when I suggest that they are probably in receipt of a large number of telegrams from people in my area and the surrounding countryside.
I am not going to read the telegrams which I have received in regard to this matter but I would like to state briefly the substance of one of them which I think will give this house an idea of the seriousness of the situation. This telegram comes from a group of potato farmers who are organized into what is called the federation of agriculture for Victoria county. Organizations such as this have been established in several counties. However, the telegram to which I have referred states that some 4,000 cars have been shipped and about 3,000 more remain to be shipped with no assurance from the marketing board that they will be handled. This telegram states that the remaining potatoes are deteriorating rapidly and will soon become unsaleable and that because of such deterioration the farmers in that area may be ruined financially. A large percentage of the farmers will be unable to plant another crop and some are now planning to get rid of their stock and machinery if possible and go out into the labour market and look for work.
After setting out these facts the organization winds up by asking that the dominion government through the Minister of Agriculture consider doing something to keep these farmers on the land so that they will be in a position to put in another crop.
4410	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Poulin
.That is the sum and substance of the situation, stated briefly. However, I would like to enlarge on that. I stated a few minutes ago that I did not dispute the fact that the cash income of farmers in Canada was greater last year than it was previously, but we are now in 1954 and the consumption of agricultural products is apparently diminishing because many people are unemployed and during this winter a great many people have been forced to live on a restricted income. It therefore has not been possible for them to eat as well as they normally would and that factor must be taken into consideration.
The Minister of Agriculture stated that cash income had doubled from something like $4,987 million during 1943 to 1945 to about $8,200 million during, I think he said, 1951 to 1953. I would have liked the minister to carry that calculation a step further and point out that while that cash income has increased the farmers' expenses have also increased. Had he done that I think it would have been demonstrated that the net result to the farmer in 1953 was that he was no better off than in 1943. They were certainly handling more money but they were not making any more. In other words, they could not put any money away, the only difference being that last year most of them put in another crop.
Last fall the New Brunswick potato farmers, following the lead of the farmers of Prince Edward Island, waited on this government and induced them to put a floor price on their potatoes, and that floor price- I think that is the way in which to state it- guaranteed a certain price. I thought that was quite a good idea and I still think so, particularly if the scheme was properly handled, but when the government undertook to do that they had to insist on the potatoes being handled by an agency, which is quite proper, and they were handled -through what is called the marketing board.
But apparently there is a lot of confusion as to whether that board has been a success. During the few days which I spent at home during the Easter recess I met quite a number of farmers who came into my town and some were quite happy about the way in which the board had handled things because they had got rid of the potatoes and they were now in a position to go ahead and put in another crop. But I must confess there were just as many farmers who had not sold any potatoes as yet and they did not speak very highly about the way in which the "board had handled the situation. I believe .there is a great deal of truth in that because I am informed that someone in the department insisted that the board handle this


potato business in a more equitable manner. If that is so I congratulate the officials of the department for keeping on the job. Since they started the quota there has been some improvement in the situation but unfortunately it was too late in the season in the case of those farmers who are still holding potatoes.
Three thousand cars of potatoes from the last week in April until the end of the season represent a large quantity of potatoes. These farmers are, as you may say, getting panicky. I know that many of the officials feel that these potatoes will be handled between now and the end of the season, but there is no assurance of that outcome. That is why these farmers are getting panicky. It is coming right now to the time when they should be starting new crops. A lot of these men are equipped to grow only potatoes. It is a potato area; it is potato land. They have the equipment for potatoes and they cannot easily switch to anything else. They seem to be faced with one of two situations: either to try to get credit to put in another crop, hoping that next year will be a good year-and about one in three or four usually is-or to sell their equipment and go out and try to get work on the labour market. I say that is an unfortunate situation.
I understand that the Minister of Agriculture also has received pleas from some of the municipalities. I can understand that. While I was in my own municipality, at Easter, as I still have a connection with the council I was called in in consultation with regard to loans. The county which is my own municipality is not what you would call a poor municipality. Its credit has been good. It is one of the good farming areas in New Brunswick. But I should like to point out this fact for the benefit of the members of this government who have been asked to give consideration to these pleas. The loans in the said municipality of Carleton are 100 per cent higher today- or they were when I was home-than they have ever been in the history of the county, even in the darkest days of the depression. The bank has been asked to get extra authority from its head office in order to make further loans to carry on until the end of June. If the farmers cannot carry on, they cannot pay their accounts.
A few minutes ago my hon. friend was speaking about the responsibility of municipal governments and the load of taxation. I should just like to confirm what he said from my own experience in my own municipality. Unless things pick up with regard to potatoes-and they are about the only

thing out of which the people in my constituency are able to get money-and the accounts are settled up before August 1, a good many schools in my municipality will not open because I do not think you can expect the school teachers to go in and teach school unless they are sure of their pay. I am sorry to say this, and I am not crying blue ruin. However, I have enough experience to know how much money it takes in that municipality to run the schools, and I know that enough taxes will not be paid in by the first of September to keep all the schools going.
I am stating these facts, Mr. Speaker, and I have taken the floor to review this situation in order to impress it upon the government and upon our own minister from New Brunswick; I refer to the Minister of Labour. I think he understands the situation fairly well. While hon. members from other parts of Canada may say that you are subsidizing potatoes from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, I think it is important that you consider going a step further this spring and consider doing something for these farmers who have not been able to get rid of their potatoes or who will not be able to do so, in order to put them in the same position as are those who got rid of their potatoes.
Here is my reason for saying that. When you gave the guarantee last fall to the farmers through the marketing board you assumed some responsibility at least in so far as the farmers are concerned. I feel that you assumed a moral responsibility to see that every farmer who wished to sell his potatoes was treated fairly and equitably. I say that for this reason. The minute the board took over under this government's guarantee the dealers had no choice of free selling. The board bought the potatoes and controlled the orders. You took the competition-if you like to put it that way-away from the dealers. In other years when the market has been free and open and private enterprise has been handling the crop it has always been disposed of and the farmers never became panicky as they have this spring.
I am not saying that the board is not going to be able to dispose of this crop. I am not here criticizing that marketing board. When the board started operations last fall I lent it what little support I could among my constituents. I have stood behind it, and I still hope it turns out to be good. But this is what I want to impress upon this government and the members of it. These people are up against a serious situation and they do not feel like waiting to see whether the
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery board is going to be able to take this stock. They are looking to you for some guarantee that the board will be able to handle it and that if the board falls down on handling it you will come to their rescue.
I say that for this reason, and I wish to repeat it. Had the board handled this whole transaction in an equitable manner, every farmer would have got rid of a certain percentage or all of his potatoes and if some potatoes were left in the cellars or the storehouses of farmers, every farmer would have been treated in the same manner. They would all have some, and then there would have been no kick. But when one man who has
3,000	to 4,000 barrels of potatoes to sell is allowed to get rid of them and another man, maybe his neighbour, who has 2,000 to 3,000 barrels of potatoes to sell has not sold them and has no prospects right away of selling them, that situation does not seem to be fair and equitable. That was the way, up until May 1, that the situation was lining up, as far as I can understand it. That is the reason there have been so many telegrams coming to the government or at least that is why the assistance is being asked for by the farmers for the balance of this season.
I do not think it is necessary for me to dwell any longer on this matter. I know that the potato business is full of rumours. No doubt the department here in Ottawa has heard all sorts of stories. No doubt you may think that some of these telegrams contain exaggerated statements. However, I know that the potato business is a tricky business. On behalf of these people in my constituency back home I want to impress upon hon. members the fact that unless they get a chance to get credit in order to put in another crop, a great many of them are going to be in just the situation described in one of the telegrams. They are going to be on the road. They are going to be out looking for a job in the labour market; and goodness knows there are not too many jobs available in the labour market. In these times no farmer should be forced to sell his machinery, to leave his farm or to go out and leave it unworked in order to make a living. I do not think that is good business. I say that this government is morally responsible because of the fact that they entered into an agreement with the marketing board.
I think you should have gone a step further and insisted that the marketing board treat all farmers alike. If you had done so, I do not think the farmers would have had any kick. But now you should do the best you can and give some direction to the board that they must handle all these potatoes in one way or another so that all farmers will

The Budget-Mr. Roy
be able to get rid of their potatoes and will be treated alike. If it does not work out satisfactorily then you can decide whether you want to carry on another year. I hope that the marketing board will become a successful institution. However, there is one thing against it. It takes away from the dealers the competition of selling and it may not turn out to be as good as we had hoped it would.
I think the Minister of Labour is going to hear more about it from the people in Victoria county, if he has not already, and also the Minister of Agriculture. I impress upon the government the necessity of doing something for these people because I feel that the government went into it in good faith and really led the farmers to believe in it. I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture has entered the house. I wish he had been here a few minutes ago, but he can read what I said. It was not very much. In part I was praising him for what he did and in part I was criticizing him for not insisting that the board do equitable work. I do not think you had to do it, but I do think that if you had taken hold of the allotment of orders sooner we would not have been in the position we are today.
I hope that the board will prove to be a success, but in order to make it a success I think the government has to give serious consideration to some of these pleas. As I said a few minutes ago, while you may feel that some of these statements are exaggerated, I know all about the potato business and I am afraid there is more truth in them than I like to believe. I happen to know that the loans of municipalities in this constituency have reached serious proportions. If there is anything you can do to give assurance to these people, get them out of their panicky condition and carry them through this season I am sure they will appreciate it.

Mr. Speaker, since this is the first time I have an opportunity to speak in this house, I would not like to depart from that excellent custom which would have me join every member of this house in congratulating Mr. Speaker (Mr. Beaudoin) and yourself, Mr. Deputy Speaker, upon your elevation to your present high posts and upon the dignity and competence brought by you to the discharge of your duties.
You will no doubt allow me to continue in this vein and to congratulate also the new ministers and parliamentary assistants, and

more particularly the hon. Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) and the member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works.
Mr. Speaker, from the few observations I have been able to make on the proceedings of this house, I have concluded that hon. members take advantage of two debates to say a few words on the importance of their constituencies: the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and the budget debate.
My riding is especially known because it sent to this house two great parliamentarians, two outstanding political figures, two great Canadians and two great autonomists. The first one, a father of confederation, Louis Joseph Papineau, and the second, an uncompromising advocate of the rights granted by this very confederation, Henri Bourassa.
A fervent patriot, a sincere and honest autonomist, Henri Bourassa, that great French Canadian political figure, left in the minds of my constituents, whom he worthily represented for several years, a political spiritual heritage they will preserve for a long time through future generations. Surely if Henri Bourassa were today at this desk, he would express all his satisfaction with the accomplishments which have resulted from ideas he suggested and vigorously advocated a quarter of a century ago. In all his independence, he would congratulate with me the present government for having implemented almost all along the line, in less than twenty years, the ideals he advocated; for having such ideals, suggested and debated hardly thirty years ago, they called him a utopian, a dreamer, and considered him unbalanced.
He would be proud and happy today to commend the St. Laurent government for the repatriation of the constitution, for the appointment of a Canadian governor general, for bringing about our complete independence from foreign ties, for the achievement of this great national unity prevailing among all Canadians. He would rejoice with me to see that an almost complete national unity may soon bring about the acceptance of a purely Canadian flag, the proclamation of a single national anthem, O Canada, and the early appointment of an ambassador to the Vatican.
But I wonder, these days, what Henri Bourassa would think of federal-provincial relations and of the thorny problem raised by the Quebec government with regard to

provincial rights to direct taxation and their corollary, the deduction of the provincial income tax from the federal tax.
No doubt, this question seems to give rise to an issue that is difficult to solve, and since both governments concerned, i.e. the governments in Ottawa and Quebec, seem to have the same rights, I think my illustrious predecessor would dare suggest to the Ottawa government that it should again, under the circumstances, make the first conciliating gesture, in order to find a point of agreement and bring about tangible and profitable results for the Quebec taxpayer as well as for the national and provincial Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, with the exception of this last controversy, it seems that this budget has not generated too much deception or too much enthusiasm and that, generally speaking, the Canadian people recognize obligingly enough that Canada has had, for several years, an excellent finance minister (Mr. Abbott). We have therefore some reason to share once again the optimism reflected in this last budget.
However, may I suggest to the Minister of Finance to restrain his overenthusiastic advisers who propose to levy a tax on mutual fire insurance companies. In my riding, there are a few of these mutual companies which have every reason to complain and to try to prevent this unjust and unfortunate measure proposed by the Minister of Finance, since the carrying out of the sixth budget resolution would have disastrous consequences for the farmers of my constituency. And I am sure that if the Minister of Finance, with the help of the appropriate experts, goes to the bottom of the question, he will easily discover that these mutual societies are nothing but co-operative enterprises which have nothing to do whatsoever with the insurance business. They are no more than organized charity institutions. They are not looking for profits; on the contrary they involve the collective responsibility of their members. The fact that in some provinces, these mutual organizations have become profit-minded corporations is proof of the generalization of this transformation. If it is right to tax the first group, there must be some way to do it without annoying in any way those of us who remained faithful to the spirit which inspired their foundation.
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the Farm Improvement Loans Act be amended or that those entrusted with
The Budget-Mr. Roy
its administration be made to pay less attention to red tape and show more interest in the excellent principles upon which the measure is based, so that the farmers from Quebec, and those of my riding in particular, may be able to benefit in greater numbers therefrom.
Mr. Speaker, the three main sources of revenue in my riding are agriculture, timber and the tourist trade. Because of the fluctuations of our markets and of the international situation, our agriculture is more or less stable, and our lumbering operations leave our forest workers all the time in a state of anxiety and insecurity.
Those two industries have to rely on a third one, the tourist trade, to balance their budget.
Sometime ago I read in an American sports and tourist magazine an article by an economist who stated that if Canada, and more particularly the province of Quebec, earmarked 50 per cent of its budget for the organization of the tourist trade in the vast areas so richly endowed by nature, in ten years the revenue from the tourist trade would double their annual budget and permit them to do away with most taxes, and more particularly with the 15 per cent income tax.
Before the war, and during the economic depression in Canada, the various governmental organizations in Ottawa had put forward several suggestions and projects to build up that profitable tourist trade. Billions of dollars are within our reach; we only have to extend the hand to get them. In my constituency, we have been endowed with natural beauties and advantages and we are only awaiting the funds which the government may decide to earmark for the organization and development of that trade, which would increase the standard of living of my constituents and make them prosperous, while paying dividends that would greatly compensate the government for its investment. Moreover, the expansion of the tourist trade would solve the unemployment problem which, in my constituency, is sufficiently serious to entail material and moral consequences, which the government should remedy.
Naturally those disturbances make themselves felt in various ways on our human resources and more particularly by a decline of health standards. I take pleasure in congratulating the government and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin)
4414	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Poulin for the progress made in the field of national health, but I always find it strange that a nation which spends two billions yearly for destructive purposes still has such a high rate of mortality, so many handicapped, so many people who suffer through lack of appropriate medical care because they cannot afford it.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the government whether the time might not be ripe to set up a compulsory health insurance scheme for that large number of Canadians who cannot afford to be sick.
Health insurance could be set up by stages, adding, one after the other, the various categories of medical needs, starting however with medical and hospitalization costs in the obstetric and pediatric group, according to age and severity of illness.
Mr. Speaker, in the same line of thought, I congratulate the government, which will introduce a measure granting assistance to the disabled, adding another stone to the structure of our generous social security system and bringing our country a step closer to the social and economic objectives which consist in the elimination of inequalities in the distribution of revenue, thus ensuring a means of livelihood to vast categories of people.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say in concluding my remarks that as long as Canada will be under this administration which has been in power for the last twenty years, all Canadians may have faith in their country, in its development, as well as in its wealth and continued prosperity.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the debate on the main motion is brought to a close, I would like to say a word on the budget resolutions introduced here on April 6 last, and more particularly on resolution No. 6, which is of interest to me since it is suggested that the surplus of mutual fire insurance companies be liable to taxation as though they were ordinary business concerns.
Of course, much could be made of the peculiar situation brought about in this respect by a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which decided, in 1953, in a test case, that the Department of National Revenue, according to the terms of the Income Tax Act, had no right to levy taxes on that type of company. Following that judgment, which was only an interpretation of the law, the government have, on second thought, undertaken to change the act, to tighten its mesh, so to speak, in order to entrap certain groups of taxpayers who, so far, had got away scot free.


This change, if it is passed by the house, will oblige mutual fire insurance companies to pay taxes on the amounts paid in by the members to make up a reserve in order to face disastrous conditions which will certainly come about sooner or later.
I see two vital differences between the position of mutual insurance corporations and that of capital stock fire insurance corporations. First of all, what is taxed in the case of ordinary insurance companies are real profits, and the most apparent effect of the tax in this case is that the shareholders and not necessarily the policyholders will receive lesser profits, less substantial dividends, and premiums will not be necessarily increased. On the contrary, in the case of mutual insurance corporations, it is no longer profits which are being taxed, but rather expenses: it is the policyholders' premiums and these, of necessity, will have to be increased.
As a matter of fact, the amounts which make up the reserve and which would be taxable, under resolution 6, come only from the premiums paid in by the policyholders, and those premiums are collected in order to pay strictly administrative costs in addition to compensations allowed the policyholders in case of fire.
It is impossible to find in all this anything in the nature of a profit. This is a protection sold at cost, and how can one make a profit when one sells at cost?
I may be asked: if there is no profit, how can there be an accumulated reserve fund? This reserve fund is only meant to facilitate operations.
In principle, each member of a mutual company has, in case of a fire, to pay his share to compensate the victim of disaster. It is understandable that the larger the number of members, the slower and more expensive the operation of collecting contributions. In order to take care of this situation, the premium is collected once or twice a year. In other words, the member is made to pay his quota, or mutual contributions, in advance, instead of having to pay it at the time the disaster happens.
As the contribution is solely used for the compensation of disaster victims, and not for paying out profits to the shareholders, it is necessary to wait for a fire to happen before using it. That is why the amounts are put aside and accumulated for the bad days, and are called a reserve fund. Where is the profit item in all this?

Secondly, in the case of mutual companies, the eventual amount of compensation to be paid is difficult to determine in advance, since the company must base its calculations on a relatively limited number of members. Thus, the 309 mutual companies of the province of Quebec have an average of a little less than 300 members each. Capital stock companies, on the other hand, can rely on an infinitely wider membership. In this case it becomes easy to determine probable standards which will deviate but little from the line generally followed by the number of disasters. And it is exactly for that reason that those large companies have a reserve fund, the amount of which varies very little from year to year while, often enough, the so-called reserve of the mutual companies may be seen to melt suddenly-which would truly be the case-in a fire of major proportions.
Does the government want the farmers to go back to the old method of passing the hat every time one of them is hit by a fire? No doubt, that practice led to splendid demonstrations of a sometimes extraordinary sense of devotion. In fact, this practice is fortunately still in existence in many localities. However, one must not forget that things have changed since those heroic times. Our farmers have grouped themselves into organizations, the same way our workers did, by the way, and it would be unfair, I believe, to penalize them for doing so by taxing the manner in which, in a modern way, they have put to use their good old spirit of mutual aid and of mutual support.
Moreover why should mutual companies dealing with fire insurance be treated in a different manner from mutual companies dealing with life insurance?
During the last few days I have received letters, telegrams or resolutions in which eleven or twelve mutual organizations established in my riding of Beauce voiced their protests. Also, last week end, I had a visit, at home, from the official delegates of three or four other companies who expressed verbally their opposition to the project.
All told, 15 or 16 such mutual societies in Beauce county have officially protested against the government's intention to tax them. I therefore pass on very humbly to the house these protests and I beg the government not to give effect to the project embodied in the sixth resolution of the present budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three questions come to my mind in considering the budget from the maritime point of view. They are prompted
The Budget-Mr. Bell by the Minister of Finance's cheerless and pessimistic words with respect to the budget. His statement that present indications point to an early uptrend in business might in itself be considered fairly hopeful for us, but the past records of optimism of the government immediately defeats that in our minds. Further words that the outlook for export trade was uncertain and much depended on the United States were also disappointing to us. Added to this is the constitutional aspect that has developed out of the debate so far. And, surprisingly, we in the maritimes are interested in the British North America Act and its various interpretations.
These questions that come to my mind are, firstly, just what is the economic condition in the maritimes? Secondly, what are our rights and claims with respect to the British North America Act and, thirdly, what course of action might be taken? First of all, I should like to discuss briefly the economic condition of the maritimes. If there should be anyone here who has any doubt that we are in a bad financial strait in the maritimes I wish that he would be attentive while I review some facts pertinent to this point. In 1871 in the maritimes we had a population of 770,000 out of a total of 3-T million. We made up one-fifth of the population of Canada. Now we make up one-eleventh. Saint John, my home town, at that time was the fourth largest city in the dominion; now we are the eighteenth and according to the last census our population has decreased 1,000.
To my mind the weekly wage rate is a key figure. I go through the Canada Year Book and I see these figures which indicate to me that we are not even holding our own in this respect. These are the weekly wage rate figures. In 1947, Prince Edward Island's was $24.75; Ontario, $38.57 and British Columbia, $41.55. The average weekly earnings in 1949, the last figures available, show Prince Edward Island with an increase of $5.01 to $29.76; Ontario had increased by $5.77 to $44.34 and British Columbia had the greatest increase of all, $5.81 to $47.36. While these figures might seem small, they are significant to me in this respect. At confederation the per capita trade figures for Ontario were $35. These are interprovincial trade figures that were kept at that time. They are not available now, but they do give us some comparison. New Brunswick surprisingly had a per capita trade figure of $56. That will give hon. members an idea of the trend since that time. The last figures for personal income show the maritimes at $804 and Ontario at $1,409.
A report on the economic condition of the maritimes is not complete, Mr. Speaker,
4416	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Bell *without some consideration of present-day problems. The first one that comes to my mind is the unemployment situation. In Saint John the unemployment figures were 2,600 at Christmastime, 3,400 at the time of pur unemployment debate and they are 4,200 now. In other words, the peak is not over in Saint John even though there may be some national trend different from that. Construction has been slow to come around and improvements in that picture will not be seen for some time.
The Marysville picture is still bad, with 385 people still out of work, according to the April 21 publication of the Fredericton Gleaner. Sixty-seven employees have been laid off by the Canadian National Railways in Moncton. The short Montreal closed season has hindered Halifax and Saint John. The other day I saw where some reliable labour group had estimated the unemployment in the maritimes at 20 per cent; whereas we know the Canadian figures are only 11 per cent.
Before leaving the economic picture of the maritimes I should like to quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail of July 17, 1953. It is an article entitled: "Canada's stepchildren". It commended itself very highly to me as a very fair appraisal of the maritime situation. The subheading is: "Maritimes too dependent on Ottawa". I should say that it is written by Richard J. Needham. This reads:
But the fact remains that the economy of that area-
Referring to the maritimes.
-is not in sound shape; that wages, and hence living standards, are substantially below the national average; that, as the financial editor of the Toronto Star put it a year ago, they are cut off from the rest of Canada by a sort of economic iron curtain. The fact remains that for all the money Ottawa has pumped into the maritimes since confederation, they are still unhealthily dependent on it.
And so I leave those figures of the economic situation in the maritimes with hon. members; and I throw out the challenge that if anybody can show me that we are even holding our own down there, I will be appreciative of it.
The second question that comes to my mind concerns our so-called maritime rights. This matter is very thoroughly dealt with in the report of the royal commission on maritime claims, commonly known as the Duncan report. This commission was headed by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, and sat in 1926.
I believe the findings are still true today. Perhaps some of the suggestions for the future have changed a bit, but a complete analysis of the picture is still pertinent, and
IMr. Bell.]

I recommend it to anyone who might be at all interested in the position of the maritime provinces. Many of these specific claims are dealt with in that report.
I should like to refer to four of those claims. The actual money grants were dealt with most thoroughly this afternoon by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). He referred to the claims that those of us in the maritimes believe we have, in view of the additions to territory in Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. Original agreements were made at the time of confederation- and I refer to both written and unwritten contracts. Before the actual contract was signed there was an understanding with the maritime provinces whereby, due to the fact that they could not possibly have territorial expansion, they would be allowed to share in the additions to the north enjoyed by the provinces I have mentioned. This matter is dealt with very thoroughly, and perhaps hon. members can guess at the results in that respect.
Then, in the matter of tax rentals, may I say I feel strongly about the way this matter was handled by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he was in Saint John in the election campaign last year. Statements were made to the effect that the government in Ottawa wished to be very generous with the maritime provinces in the matter of tax rentals because it was felt we had a claim to some of the money due to the fact that the head offices of our large corporations are located centrally. Well, that is the very thing to which we are objecting. We definitely want to have some of the head offices of businesses down our way so that it will not be a case of giving a handout every time we go after extra considerations.
Then the development of trade is another matter that confronts us vividly in the maritime provinces. Halifax and Saint John have suffered because of the Montreal season to which I referred a short time ago. Yet no efforts are being made by the central government even to try to regain United Kingdom trade. I feel that with Mr. Peter Thorneycroft and his group coming out to Canada in a short time we should get down to business and talk to them in an effort to regain this United Kingdom trade that is so very vital to the welfare of the eastern provinces.
Then there is one further matter, that of migration. We all know the story of the maritimers who have gone out west and done well. It is all very fine to be able to say that a premier of British Columbia is a New Brunswicker or that a prime minister of Great Britain was from the maritimes, or a justice of the supreme court in one of the

other provinces is from the maritimes. That sounds good; but I say that we are losing our future if the best men in our eastern provinces have to go out west or to other places.
Finally I should like to deal with the course of action that might be taken by us in trying to correct this situation. The first suggestion I would make would be to forget the sectionalism that exists in the maritimes. I think we could take a fine example from western members who, when the wheat problem is under review, drop all their other interests and get behind the discussion of that problem. I remember speaking to a western member only today. I know that he has no connection with wheat farmers and that he is entirely independent of the wheat situation. However, he said to me, "I have to go down and speak about the wheat situation". That is a lesson for those of us from the maritimes.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) who comes from New Brunswick is interested in the Passamaquoddy project. Then, the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) has spoken fluently about the Chignecto canal. At the present time I favour the Beechwood project. But I would say this, that we have to get together. I would not mind sacrificing interests or sectional ideas I might have if I felt that we could put our weight behind the suggestions we make. My weight might not be as great as some others who are in a better situation; but I believe that if we would speak up, as the western members do, we would be listened to.
Then my second suggestion is most appropriate in this debate on the budget, because I would refer to the situation at Marysville. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) spoke glowingly the other day in the committee on industrial relations about the plan they have to correct the situation down there, which has been brought about by the shutdown in the textile mills. We appreciate his efforts; nevertheless I feel it is my duty to say that those efforts are not being directed in the right way. The situation in Marysville can be corrected only by bringing new industry to Marysville. Vocational training for those who are there is all very well; but there must be industry for them to go to.
In this respect I believe we could take a lesson from the New England states. In their bargaining over support of the St. Lawrence seaway I understand some of the states have asked, and been assured they will get, consideration for their surplus labour areas. Another thing that was asked for, and might be worthy of consideration, was an acceptance by the government of a certain
The Budget-Mr. Bell type of depreciation over a number of years, in an effort to induce new industries to locate in these surplus labour towns. In other words, assessments do not have to be lowered by the localities, but the federal government should be willing to depreciate by a special method of low-cost depreciation that would induce industries to locate in towns such as Marysville. I feel that would be a step in the right direction.
I have already pointed out the importance of trade to us in Halifax and Saint John, and I shall leave a suggestion in this connection. ,
I think we should investigate and consider very seriously the possibilities of making; Saint John and Halifax free ports. In the United States today they already have free trading zones, and I know that San Francisco, New York, and New Orleans have had considerable success from this business of foreign trade zones. These foreign trade zones in the United States do not replace other shipping and receiving facilities. They provide extraordinary additional services the greatest of which in many cases develop trade which otherwise would not be able to move. This development of new trade in commodities which had not heretofore entered the United States is deemed to be of prime advantage in assisting, expediting and stimulating foreign trade.
These are the views I leave with you, Mr. Speaker, and in reviewing the matter I would like to say that I have emphasized three questions which came to my mind in first considering the budget. The first of these is, just what is the economic picture in the maritimes? Secondly, what are our rights under the confederation agreements? And thirdly, what course of action might be taken to get some form of agreement such as our western friends seem to be able to obtain? In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from this report of the royal commission on maritime claims which I have-already mentioned. The words here are very appropriate and I think they hit the nail on the head as far as the maritimes are concerned in relation to the dominion. I quote-from page 11 of the report which reads as follows:
The maritime provinces today are different in the structure of their enterprise from what they were in 1867, and their potentialities are even greater today than they were then. Confederation, too, is no longer an experiment. Its achievements in the complicated art of nation-building have brought it to a point of development which more than justifies the hopes and the vision of the early builders. The maritime provinces have produced, in every walk of life, men who have played a high part in the story of achievement. We believe that the claim which these provinces have submitted . . . and the future possibilities of their own part of the dominion, should now be reviewed with

The Budget-Mr. Holowach
sympathetic consideration and understanding, so that in approaching the future a better balance of territorial prosperity can be assured, and the -original hope of confederation-unity, prosperity and contentment for all the provinces, as well as for the whole of Canada-can be made capable of realization.

Mr. Speaker, the budget debate at present taking place in this house offers opportunities to hon. members to express their views on certain matters which [DOT]otherwise may not arise in the ordinary course of the proceedings and which do not generally come under discussion. But listening to other hon. members taking part in this debate, and reviewing the subject matter [DOT]of the serious problems which are brought to 'the attention of the government, I am amazed that up to this time no one has touched on a problem which is surely of concern to all hon. members because it involves a matter of great importance in the rapid growth of this young country.
Looking at a map of the world and Canada's location thereon in terms of its relation to neighbouring countries we cannot help but notice that Canada covers a vast area and is geographically in a strategic position. It is only a few flying hours from our neighbours to the north and northwest. In addition to its strategic position its territories contain vast resources of strategic materials. Space is another thing that we have in great abundance in Canada and while that in a sense is a blessing, when one considers the possibilities of expansion and growth, it

must be borne in mind that our cities and our people are widely scattered and distance carries with it serious liabilities.
In this regard I would like to deal with the problem of the ever-increasing needs for commercial roads and highways throughout our country. There has been very little discussion during this session of parliament on this topic other than the proposed assistance in the construction of the trans-Canada highway project. Highways and roads are of great importance to Canada and I consider it my duty to express views on this "down to earth" subject and introduce for the serious consideration of the government the need for further financial aid to the provinces, particularly in the matter of building certain interprovincial highways which, because of their military significance, are important for the entire country.
It is realized, Mr. Speaker, that the function of building and maintaining highways and roads falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but when roads affect the social, economic, cultural and indeed the security and lives of Canadians then I do believe that a certain measure of this responsibility must fall upon the shoulders of the senior government.
